'Dignity of the individual' and 'unity and integrity of the Nation' go with Fraternity.

POL-6.1.6-P57-01.lead: Sovereignty means India decides its own internal and foreign affairs.
points: Commonwealth membership is voluntary; it puts no external authority over India.
India is a republic: its head of State is the elected President, not the British monarch.
India accepts the monarch only as the symbolic Head of the Commonwealth (1949 London Declaration).

POL-6.1.6-P58-01.lead: Article 25(2)(a) lets the State regulate secular activities linked to religion.
points: Financial, economic and political activities associated with religious practice can be regulated by law.
Religious freedom is subject to public order, morality, health and other Fundamental Rights; it is not absolute.
No constitutional amendment is needed, and India has no officially recognised religion.

POL-6.1.6-P58-02.lead: In representative democracy, elected representatives make laws for the people.
points: India mainly uses indirect (representative) democracy; national referendums are not part of the system.
Hereditary succession to legislative office goes against democracy.
Members of Parliament and State legislatures are elected by voters, not chosen by judges.

POL-6.1.6-P59-01.lead: Politics participation = political, caste removal = social, income gap = economic justice.
points: Correct code: 1–c, 2–b, 3–a.

POL-6.1.6-P60-01.lead: Article 325 bars separate electoral rolls on religion, race, caste or sex.
points: Article 325 ended the colonial system of separate electorates.

POL-6.1.6-P61-01.lead: The Preamble helps interpret ambiguous provisions but is not enforceable by itself.

POL-631-N002.also: Fraternity assures dignity of the individual and unity and integrity of the Nation.

Article 1 calls India a 'Union of States', not a federation.

POL-631-P56-02.lead: 'We, the People of India' shows the people are the source of authority.

POL-631-P56-03.lead: Nandalal Bose led the art; Sinha did the Preamble page; Raizada wrote it.

POL-631-P57-02.lead: Indian socialism is democratic: public and private sectors coexist.

POL-631-P60-04.lead: Preamble is amendable under Article 368, but its basic features cannot be destroyed.

POL-631-P61-02.lead: LIC case (1995) reaffirmed the Preamble as an integral part of the Constitution.

POL-6.1.9-P100-08.lead: Major General S.R. Sinho Commission submitted its report on 22 July 2010.
points: The Sinho Commission was set up in 2006; its work formed background to the 103rd Amendment.

POL-6.1.9-P100-09.lead: Indra Sawhney struck down the 10% economic quota as invalid.
points: The Court held economic criteria alone cannot be the basis of reservation under Article 16(4).
The OBC 27% part (clause i) was upheld with creamy-layer exclusion.
EWS reservation later came through the 103rd Amendment (2019) by changing the Constitution.

POL-6.1.9-P100-10.lead: Limits are 'below ₹8 lakh' and 'below 200 sq yards', so exactly-at-limit excludes.
points: Income must be below ₹8 lakh; exactly ₹8 lakh fails.
Plots of 200 sq yards and above outside notified municipalities exclude the family.
So both grounds independently exclude the applicant.

POL-6.1.9-P100-11.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct; Article 16(6) excludes Article 16(4) classes.

POL-6.1.9-P100-12.lead: Article 371D was added by the 32nd Amendment Act, 1973.
points: It gives special provisions for Andhra Pradesh on jobs and education.
The 7th Amendment (1956) reorganised States; the 42nd (1976) added 'Socialist' and 'Secular'.
The 103rd Amendment (2019) gave EWS reservation.
POL-6.1.9-P100-12.also: Article 371E (Central University in AP) was also added by the 32nd Amendment.

POL-6.1.9-P101-01.lead: All three statements about the Mandal Commission are correct.
points: It identified 3,743 backward castes as OBCs.

POL-6.1.9-P101-02.lead: Mandal used 11 indicators under social, educational and economic heads.
points: Social: 4 indicators; educational: 3; economic: 4.
Social indicators carried 3 points each, educational 2, economic 1.

POL-6.1.9-P101-03.lead: Mandal recommended 27% reservation for OBCs in Central posts.
points: It estimated OBCs at about 52% of the population.
27% was fixed so total reservation stays within 50% along with SC and ST 22.5%.
10% was the economic quota later struck down in Indra Sawhney.

POL-6.1.9-P101-04.lead: Indra Sawhney held the creamy layer must be excluded from OBC benefits.
points: Being in an OBC community is not enough; advanced members are left out.
This is applied to the individual, even if the community stays on the OBC list.
Creamy-layer status has nothing to do with unreserved posts; anyone can compete there.
POL-6.1.9-P101-04.also: Indra Sawhney (1992) also fixed the 50% ceiling on reservations.

POL-6.1.9-P101-05.lead: Jarnail Singh dropped the backwardness-data test, not the representation-data test.
points: Jarnail Singh (2018) was a 5-judge Bench reviewing M. Nagaraj (2006).
It also held creamy layer exclusion can apply to SC/ST in promotions.

POL-6.1.9-P101-06.lead: The 2019 amendment cut the Maratha quota to 12% (education) and 13% (jobs).
points: The 2018 SEBC Act originally gave 16% in both.
Bombay High Court (2019) upheld it but reduced it to 12% and 13%; the 2019 amendment adopted these.
The Supreme Court struck down both in May 2021.
POL-6.1.9-P101-06.also: The Bench of 5 judges also held, by 3:2, that after the 102nd Amendment only the Centre could identify SEBCs (later undone by the 105th Amendment, 2021).

POL-6.1.9-P101-07.lead: The Court kept the 50% ceiling and found no extraordinary case for Marathas.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: True — Marathas not such a case

points: The Court refused to refer Indra Sawhney (1992) to a larger Bench.

POL-6.1.9-P101-08.lead: Creamy-layer income limit went from ₹6 lakh to ₹8 lakh in 2017.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — parents' post and property also count

points: Children of parents holding high constitutional posts or Group A posts fall in creamy layer regardless of income.

POL-6.1.9-P101-09.lead: Nagaraj upheld all four amendments but laid down conditions for using them.
points: The amendments only enable the State; they do not compel reservation in promotion.
Conditions: backwardness data, inadequate representation, and overall efficiency (Article 335).
Options 1 and 2 are wrong: none was struck down. Option 3 is wrong: policies still face judicial review.
POL-6.1.9-P101-09.also: 77th (1995) inserted Art 16(4A); 81st (2000) inserted Art 16(4B); 82nd (2000) amended Art 335; 85th (2001) added consequential seniority.

POL-6.1.9-P102-01.lead: Sub-classification is allowed, but only Parliament can change the SC list.

head: Part
Claim
True/False — why
rows: States may sub-classify SCs with data

points: Sub-classification shares benefits within the listed SCs; it does not add or remove castes.
It needs empirical data on inadequate representation and is open to judicial review.
POL-6.1.9-P102-01.also: It overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004). Justice Bela Trivedi dissented.

POL-6.1.9-P102-02.lead: The 1976 amendment changed the name, but the year stays 1955.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — it is the PCR Act, 1955

points: The Act enforces Article 17, which abolishes untouchability.
POL-6.1.9-P102-02.also: SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act is a separate law of 1989.

POL-6.1.9-P102-03.lead: Article 18(1) bars State titles except military and academic distinctions.
points: Hereditary, political or religious distinctions are not excepted.
So the State can award ranks like General or degrees like Doctor, but not titles like 'Raja'.
POL-6.1.9-P102-03.also: Article 18 has four clauses: (1) State conferring, (2)–(3) foreign titles, (4) foreign presents/office.

POL-6.1.9-P102-04.lead: Citizens can never accept foreign titles; only non-citizen office-holders need President's consent.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Citizen may accept with President's consent
False — Art 18(2) is an absolute ban

POL-6.1.9-P102-05.lead: Article 18(4) covers any present, emolument or office from a foreign State.
points: It applies to any person, citizen or not, holding an office of profit or trust under the State.
Accepting any of the three from or under a foreign State needs the President's consent.

POL-6.1.9-P102-06.lead: Untouchability means caste-based exclusion treated as ritual pollution.

head: No.
Situation
Untouchability?
rows: Barred from public well due to caste

points: Article 17 is not defined in the Constitution; courts read it in its historical caste sense.
Article 17 applies against private persons too.

POL-6.1.9-P102-07.lead: Article 17 abolishes untouchability itself; the punishment comes from law.
points: Option 1 is wrong: abolition took effect with the Constitution, no further law needed.
Option 2 is wrong: Article 17 fixes no sentence; Parliament makes laws under Article 35.
Option 3 is wrong: States have no choice; the ban is absolute.
POL-6.1.9-P102-07.also: Laws made: Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955 (now PCR Act) and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act 1989.

POL-6.1.9-P102-08.lead: Article 18(1) bars the State from conferring titles on anyone, citizen or foreigner.
points: Option 1 is wrong: the clause says 'no title shall be conferred by the State', with no citizenship limit.
Options 3 and 4 are wrong: clauses (2) and (3) deal with accepting titles from foreign States.

POL-6.1.9-P103-01.lead: National awards are not 'titles', but cannot be used before or after names.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — misuse can lead to forfeiture

points: Balaji Raghavan v. Union of India was decided on 15 December 1995 (reported 1996).

POL-6.1.9-P103-02.lead: Five people got Bharat Ratna in 2024, the most in one year.
points: Four of the five were posthumous; Advani was the only living recipient.
POL-6.1.9-P103-02.also: The usual practice limits awards to three a year, but 2024 had five.

points: Clauses (d) movement and (e) residence come between (c) and (g); (f) property was deleted.

POL-6.1.9-P103-04.lead: Movement is Article 19(1)(d); residence and settlement is 19(1)(e).
points: Both are restricted under Article 19(5): general public interest or protection of Scheduled Tribes.
Clause (c) is association and (g) is profession, so other options mismatch.
POL-6.1.9-P103-04.also: Right to travel abroad comes under Article 21 (Maneka Gandhi, 1978), not 19(1)(d).

POL-6.1.9-P103-05.lead: 44th Amendment removed property from Part III, but law is still needed to take it.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Property can be taken without law
False — Art 300A needs authority of law

points: Article 31 was also repealed; property is now a constitutional (legal) right, not a Fundamental Right.
These changes took effect on 20 June 1979.

POL-6.1.9-P104-01.lead: Press freedom is read into free speech under Article 19(1)(a).
points: It is not separately mentioned in the Constitution.
Courts recognised it in Romesh Thappar (1950) and Sakal Papers (1962).
Option 4 is wrong: Article 19 rights belong to all citizens, not only journalists.

POL-6.1.9-P104-02.lead: 'General public interest' is not a ground in Article 19(2).
points: Article 19(2) grounds: sovereignty and integrity, security of State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order.
Others: decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence.
'Interests of the general public' appears in Article 19(5) and 19(6), not 19(2).
POL-6.1.9-P104-02.also: First Amendment (1951) added public order, friendly relations and incitement; 16th Amendment (1963) added sovereignty and integrity.

POL-6.1.9-P104-03.lead: Truthful commercial advertisements are protected speech, subject to reasonable restrictions.
points: Tata Press v. MTNL (1995) held commercial speech is part of Article 19(1)(a).
Options 1–3 are wrong: profit motive does not remove protection, and false or misleading ads can still be regulated.

POL-6.1.9-P104-04.lead: Bijoe Emmanuel protected respectful silence during the anthem for religious belief.
points: In 1986 the Supreme Court protected Jehovah's Witness students under Articles 19(1)(a) and 25.
Free speech includes the right to remain silent.
Options 2–4 are wrong: standing respectfully without singing showed no disrespect.

POL-6.1.9-P104-05.lead: Legislative speech is subject to the Constitution and House rules, and immune from courts.
points: Article 105 is for Parliament; Article 194 is for State Legislatures.

POL-6.1.9-P104-06.lead: NOTA votes are counted but cannot defeat a candidate; A wins.
points: The candidate with the most votes among the candidates is declared elected, even if NOTA gets more.
No fresh poll or disqualification follows from NOTA leading.
NOTA is not available in Rajya Sabha and Legislative Council elections.

POL-6.1.9-P104-07.lead: Airwaves are public property, so their use can be regulated.

head: Part
Claim
True/False — why
rows: No unrestricted right to any frequency

points: The 1995 judgment held the right to telecast and receive information is part of Article 19(1)(a).
POL-6.1.9-P104-07.also: It recommended an independent public authority to regulate airwaves.

POL-6.1.9-P104-08.lead: Kerala High Court linked internet access to education and privacy.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Internet linked to education and privacy
Phone use can never be regulated
False — regulation if it disturbs others

POL-6.1.9-P104-09.lead: The FIR was quashed, but the special committee plea was rejected.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — prayer rejected as legislative domain

points: The Court said every journalist is entitled to protection under Kedar Nath Singh (1962).

POL-6.1.9-P104-10.lead: A ban on all demonstrations wrongly covers peaceful protest under 19(1)(a) and (b).
points: Kameshwar Prasad (1962) struck down the Bihar rule banning all demonstrations by government servants.
Government servants keep their Fundamental Rights.
The same case held there is no fundamental right to strike.

POL-6.1.9-P104-11.lead: PUCL (2013) linked NOTA to expression and secrecy, not disclosure.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Right to vote vs freedom of voting

points: Before 2013, Rule 49-O required recording a voter's refusal, which broke secrecy.
POL-6.1.9-P104-11.also: NOTA was introduced from 2013 after this judgment (27 September 2013).

POL-6.1.9-P104-12.lead: Knowing a candidate's background helps voters make an informed choice under 19(1)(a).
points: The right to know candidates' criminal, financial and educational details was recognised in ADR (2002) and PUCL (2003).
Option 1 is wrong: secrecy protects the voter's choice, not candidate details.
Option 4 is wrong: the voting right is statutory, but expression through voting is a Fundamental Right.

POL-6.1.9-P104-13.lead: Mathew J. linked right to know to free speech, but not as absolute.
points: He said people have a right to know every public act done by public functionaries.
He accepted that genuine security concerns can justify secrecy.
Options 1, 2 and 4 are wrong: they make the right absolute, deny it, or limit it to legislators.
POL-6.1.9-P104-13.also: The right to information was later given effect by the RTI Act, 2005.

POL-6.1.9-P104-14.lead: Tapping affects privacy and speech; either emergency or public safety is enough.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Emergency and safety must both exist
Reasons to be recorded in writing

points: The Court also laid down procedural safeguards, such as orders by the Home Secretary and a review committee.
POL-6.1.9-P104-14.also: Telegraph Act, 1885 is now replaced by the Telecommunications Act, 2023.

POL-6.1.9-P104-15.lead: Kedar Nath upheld sedition, limited to incitement to violence or public disorder.
points: Strong criticism of government by lawful means was not sedition.
Options 2–4 are wrong: the law was not struck down, and speech can face reasonable penal restrictions.
POL-6.1.9-P104-15.also: In S.G. Vombatkere (May 2022) the Supreme Court put sedition cases on hold; the BNS dropped the word 'sedition'.

POL-6.1.9-P104-16.lead: 124 = assault on President/Governor; 124A = sedition; 499 = defamation; 500 = punishment.
POL-6.1.9-P104-16.also: In the BNS, defamation is Section 356.

POL-6.1.9-P104-17.lead: Section 144 was in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
points: It let Executive Magistrates issue urgent orders against nuisance or apprehended danger.
IPC and BNS are penal laws; BSA, 2023 is the evidence law.
Its successor is Section 163 of BNSS, 2023, in force from 1 July 2024.

POL-6.1.9-P104-18.lead: Kerala's 2017 Governor's address promised internet as a right, with free bandwidth.
points: Kerala planned the K-FON project to give free internet to poor households.
In 2019, the Kerala High Court (Faheema Shirin) also linked internet access to Article 21.

POL-6.1.9-P105-01.lead: Section 66A was struck down; criminal defamation was upheld.
points: Subramanian Swamy held reputation is part of Article 21.

POL-6.1.9-P105-02.lead: Vague and overbroad laws chill free speech and allow arbitrary arrests.
points: Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Section 66A for words like 'annoying' and 'inconvenient'.
Annoyance is not an Article 19(2) ground, and the internet medium adds no new ground.
Option 2 is wrong: a small penalty does not cure vagueness.

POL-6.1.9-P105-03.lead: BNS Section 152 is 'Act endangering sovereignty, unity and integrity of India'.
points: It is widely seen as replacing IPC 124A (sedition), though wording differs.

POL-6.1.9-P105-04.lead: Lawful criticism of government that excites no listed activity is not an offence.
points: The Explanation covers measures and administrative or other action of the Government.
Option 2 is wrong: action already taken is covered too.
Options 3 and 4 are wrong: no government acceptance needed, and written comments are covered.

POL-6.1.9-P105-05.lead: Courts check the offence's ingredients; mere disagreement is not a crime.
points: Khushboo (28 April 2010): SC quashed complaints over her remarks on pre-marital sex.
Option 1 wrong: public outrage alone does not make out an offence.
Option 2 wrong: Article 19(1)(a) protects unpopular views too.
Option 4 wrong: Article 19(2) still allows reasonable restrictions; no blanket immunity.
POL-6.1.9-P105-05.also: Free speech covers ideas that offend, shock or disturb some people.

POL-6.1.9-P105-06.lead: Right to form associations does not include a fundamental right to strike.
points: T.K. Rangarajan (2003): Tamil Nadu govt employees have no fundamental, legal, moral or equitable right to strike.
Option 1 wrong: the right to form a union does not guarantee every means used by it.
Options 3 and 4 wrong: silence in Article 19 or statutory permission does not create a Fundamental Right.
POL-6.1.9-P105-06.also: Earlier: All India Bank Employees (1962) — right to association does not include right to strike.

POL-6.1.9-P105-07.lead: Enforcing a bandh cannot override other citizens' fundamental freedoms.
points: CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar (1997): SC upheld Kerala HC — enforced bandhs are unconstitutional.
A bandh coerces people not to work, travel or open shops, hurting Articles 19 and 21.
Options 1–3 wrong: political aim or majority support does not cancel others' rights.
POL-6.1.9-P105-07.also: Hartal or strike call is different from a bandh that compels everyone to stop.

POL-6.1.9-P105-08.lead: Only statement 1 is right: ₹1 fine; jail and bar only if unpaid.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Jail and bar apply even if paid
False — only if fine not paid by 15 Sept 2020

POL-6.1.9-P105-08.also: Default terms: 3 months' simple imprisonment and 3-year practice bar.

points: Bharat Kumar is reported in 1998 law reports, but the decision is 12 November 1997.
Khushboo was decided on 28 April 2010; ignore later report years like 2012.

POL-6.1.9-P105-10.lead: Expression abroad is protected but subject to 19(2); 19(1)(d) is India only.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: True — free speech has no territorial limit
False — movement 'throughout the territory of India'

POL-6.1.9-P105-10.also: Right to travel abroad is part of personal liberty under Article 21 (Satwant Singh 1967, Maneka 1978).

POL-6.1.9-P106-01.lead: Public order is common to 19(3) and 19(4); morality is only in 19(4).

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Public order restricts assembly and association

POL-6.1.9-P106-01.also: 19(3) grounds: sovereignty and integrity of India, public order.

POL-6.1.9-P106-02.lead: The 97th Amendment added 'co-operative societies' to Article 19(1)(c).
POL-6.1.9-P106-02.also: 97th Amendment came into force on 15 February 2012.

POL-6.1.9-P106-03.lead: Flying the flag respectfully is free expression, but reasonable restrictions apply.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — 19(2) restrictions and flag laws still apply

POL-6.1.9-P106-03.also: Flag Code of India, 2002 and Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 regulate use.

POL-6.1.9-P106-04.lead: The 2018 order made playing the Anthem in cinemas optional, not compulsory.
points: 30 November 2016 interim order had made it compulsory before films.
9 January 2018 modified that order: playing became directory (optional).
Options 2 and 3 wrong: no ban, and respect for the Anthem remains expected when played.
POL-6.1.9-P106-04.also: Bijoe Emmanuel (1986): not singing the Anthem while standing respectfully is not an offence.

POL-6.1.9-P106-05.lead: Section 163 is in BNSS, 2023 — successor of CrPC Section 144.
POL-6.1.9-P106-05.also: The three new criminal laws came into force on 1 July 2024.

POL-6.1.9-P106-06.lead: Adults' choice of partner cannot be vetoed by a caste council.
points: Shakti Vahini (2018): SC held khap interference with consenting adults' marriage illegal.
Choosing a life partner is protected under Articles 19 and 21.
Options 1, 3, 4 wrong: community or family approval cannot override adult choice or marriage law.
POL-6.1.9-P106-06.also: Shafin Jahan (2018, Hadiya case): right to choose a partner is part of Article 21.

POL-6.1.9-P106-08.lead: Film pre-censorship is valid, but only within constitutional limits.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: True — clear guidelines, regard for art

POL-6.1.9-P106-08.also: K.A. Abbas (1970): films can be treated differently from other media due to their impact.

POL-6.1.9-P106-09.lead: Rajendra Shah kept Part IXB only for multi-State co-operatives; 19(1)(c), 43B survived.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — only Part IXB (State co-ops) struck
Part IXB kept for multi-State co-ops

POL-6.1.9-P106-09.also: Part IXB was struck for want of State ratification under Article 368(2).

POL-6.1.9-P106-10.lead: Only sovereignty-integrity and public order are common to 19(3) and 19(4).

POL-6.1.9-P106-11.lead: RTI enacted 15 June 2005; most provisions began 12 October 2005.
POL-6.1.9-P106-11.also: Sections in force at once include 4(1), 5(1), 5(2), 12, 13, 15, 16, 24, 27, 28.

POL-6.1.9-P106-12.lead: Right to form an association includes continuing it with chosen members.
points: Damyanti Naranga (1971): a law forcing new members into Hindi Sahitya Sammelan was struck down.
Option 1 wrong: protection does not end at formation.
Option 2 wrong: reasonable restrictions under 19(4) still apply.
Option 3 wrong: keeping the name while changing members defeats the right.

POL-6.1.9-P106-13.lead: Brij Bhushan majority struck down pre-censorship of a newspaper.
points: Brij Bhushan (1950): pre-publication scrutiny of 'Organiser' was a restriction on press freedom.
Original 19(2) then lacked 'public order', so the order could not be saved (options 2, 4 wrong).
Option 3 wrong: films were dealt with in K.A. Abbas (1970).
POL-6.1.9-P106-13.also: First Amendment (1951) added 'public order' to Article 19(2).

POL-6.1.9-P106-14.lead: Naveen Jindal is 2004; Seema's original marriage-registration directions are 2006.
POL-6.1.9-P106-14.also: Seema had further orders in 2007 and 2008; original directions: 14 February 2006.

POL-6.1.9-P107-01.lead: Article 19(6) lets the State prescribe professional or technical qualifications.
points: Article 19(6)(i): law may prescribe qualifications for practising a profession or trade.
Option 1 wrong: it covers private practice, not just government jobs.
Option 2 wrong: State monopoly is a separate limb, 19(6)(ii).
Option 4 wrong: educational qualifications are exactly what 19(6)(i) allows.

POL-6.1.9-P107-02.lead: Article 20(1) bars conviction under a retrospective (ex post facto) criminal law.
POL-6.1.9-P107-02.also: Article 20 cannot be suspended even during an Emergency (44th Amendment).

POL-6.1.9-P107-03.lead: No penalty greater than the law at the time of the offence (Article 20(1)).
points: Here the maximum stays two years, though the law changed before sentencing.
Options 1–3 wrong: trial date or seriousness does not allow the higher penalty.
POL-6.1.9-P107-03.also: Article 20(1) has two limbs: no ex post facto conviction, no greater penalty.

POL-6.1.9-P107-05.lead: Article 20(2) needs prosecution and punishment by a court; departmental action is not.
points: S.A. Venkataraman (1958): departmental inquiry is not 'prosecution and punishment'.
So A is true, and R gives exactly the reason.
POL-6.1.9-P107-05.also: Maqbool Hussain (1953): customs confiscation is not prosecution by a judicial tribunal.

POL-6.1.9-P107-06.lead: Compelled testimonial admissions by an accused engage Article 20(3).
points: Option 1 is Article 20(2); option 2 is Article 20(1).
Option 4 wrong: lawful fingerprints, handwriting samples are not 'being a witness' (Kathi Kalu Oghad).

POL-6.1.9-P107-07.lead: Article 19(5) names general public interest and protection of Scheduled Tribes.

POL-6.1.9-P107-08.lead: Article 19(6)(ii) allows State monopolies, fully or partly excluding citizens.
points: Added by the First Amendment (1951).
Option 2 wrong: complete exclusion is expressly allowed.
Option 3 wrong: qualifications are 19(6)(i), not (ii).
Option 4 wrong: State trade competing with or excluding citizens is permitted.

POL-6.1.9-P107-09.lead: Article 20(1) bars harsher retrospective penalty, not a lighter one.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — it only stops greater penalty
Depends on the statute and savings clause
True — courts examine the new law

POL-6.1.9-P107-09.also: T. Barai (1983): accused may get benefit of a later reduced punishment.

POL-6.1.9-P107-10.lead: Only general public interest is a stated ground in Article 19(6).

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — also State trade and public interest

POL-6.1.9-P107-11.lead: The State must protect lawful expression, not surrender to threats.
points: S. Rangarajan (1989): film 'Ore Oru Gramathiley' could not be banned over threatened protests.
Options 1, 2 wrong: threats are no valid ground; this is a 'heckler's veto'.
Option 4 wrong: disagreement does not remove protection.
POL-6.1.9-P107-11.also: Freedom of expression cannot be held to ransom by threats of violence.

POL-6.1.9-P107-12.lead: Article 20(1) does not bar later changes in procedure or trial court.
points: Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh (1953): no one has a vested right in a particular procedure.
Article 20(1) covers only conviction and penalty (options 1, 3 wrong).
Option 2 wrong: the change can still be tested under Article 14 and others.

POL-6.1.9-P108-01.lead: Article 20(1) applies only to criminal laws, not civil or tax laws.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — only criminal conviction and penalty
Tax law tested under other provisions

POL-6.1.9-P108-01.also: Parliament and legislatures can make retrospective civil and tax laws.

POL-6.1.9-P108-02.lead: A lawful fingerprint is identification material, not testimony.
points: Kathi Kalu Oghad (1961): fingerprints, signatures, handwriting samples are not 'being a witness'.
Options 1–3 are compelled testimony from personal knowledge, barred by Article 20(3).
POL-6.1.9-P108-02.also: Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022 governs taking such measurements.

POL-6.1.9-P108-03.lead: Article 20(3) protection extends to police interrogation, not just court.
points: Nandini Satpathy (1978): right to silence applies at the police stage too.
So A is true, and R explains why.
POL-6.1.9-P108-03.also: An accused includes one formally accused in an FIR at the time of statement.

POL-6.1.9-P108-04.lead: Article 21 protects every person, citizens and foreigners alike.
points: Article 21 says 'no person', not 'no citizen'.
Options 1, 2, 4 wrong: no residence, reciprocity or job condition.
POL-6.1.9-P108-04.also: Article 19 rights are only for citizens; Articles 14, 20, 21 cover all persons.

POL-6.1.9-P108-05.lead: Article 21 uses 'procedure established by law', taken from Japan.
points: 'Due process of law' is the US phrase; framers did not adopt it.
Options 3, 4: no such phrases in Article 21.
POL-6.1.9-P108-05.also: After Maneka Gandhi, procedure must be fair, just and reasonable.

POL-6.1.9-P108-06.lead: After Maneka Gandhi, procedure must be fair, just and reasonable.
points: Maneka Gandhi (1978) overruled the narrow A.K. Gopalan (1950) view.

points: RBI is not the only route; cash may be paid to the Returning Officer — option 1 wrong.

POL-R21-ELECT-deposit-sixth-boundary.lead: Deposit is forfeited unless votes exceed one-sixth; exactly one-sixth forfeits.
points: One-sixth of 60,000 is 10,000; the candidate got exactly 10,000.
Section 158(4) says deposit is forfeited if votes do 'not exceed' one-sixth.
There is no half-refund or transfer to the winner — options 2 and 4 wrong.
POL-R21-ELECT-deposit-sixth-boundary.also: Deposit is always returned to the winner and if a candidate dies before polling.

POL-R21-ELECT-expense2022.lead: Bigger States like Andhra Pradesh: ₹95 lakh; smaller States like Goa: ₹75 lakh.
points: The 2022 revision raised the Lok Sabha limit from ₹70 lakh to ₹95 lakh for most States.
Goa, Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim got the lower ₹75 lakh limit.
₹40 lakh and ₹28 lakh are Assembly limits, not Lok Sabha.

POL-R21-ELECT-financial-affidavit.lead: Form 26 covers assets and liabilities of self, spouse, HUF and dependents.
points: Form 2A is the nomination paper, not the asset affidavit — option 1 wrong.

Form 20 is the final result sheet, not a party asset statement — option 4 wrong.

POL-R21-ELECT-petition-route.lead: Candidate or elector files in High Court within 45 days; appeal lies to Supreme Court.

points: 'Demos' is Greek (people), root of 'democracy'.
'Lex' (law) and 'imperium' (command) are Latin words.

POL-R21-HIST-Provisional-Parliament.lead: The Constituent Assembly (Legislative) served as Provisional Parliament, 1950–1952.

Nominated MLAs do not vote, and people do not vote directly. First-past-the-post is not used.

POL-R21-PH-RS-constitution-first-sitting.lead: Rajya Sabha was formed on 3 April 1952 and first sat on 13 May 1952.

POL-R21-PH-corrupt-practice-voiding-cond.lead: If the winner is proved to have committed bribery, the High Court must declare the election void.

The Fifth Lok Sabha was dissolved early, and elections were held in March 1977.

POL-R21-PH-first-LS-limit-and-elected-se.lead: The original Article 81 allowed up to 500 elected members. The first election filled 489 seats.

Verdict

POL-R21-PRES-parliamentary-functions.lead: The President is part of Parliament but not a member of either House.

Art 86–87: the President may address either House or both together. Art 111: assent to Bills. Art 85(2)(b): dissolving the Lok Sabha.
The Speaker, not the President, certifies Money Bills. Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved.

POL-R21-PRIV-PV-chronology-bench.lead: The vote was in 1993 and the judgment in 1998. Five judges split 3:2 on immunity.

Option 3 describes Sita Soren (2024), but that bench was unanimous, not 4:3.

POL-R21-PRIV-PV-historical-rule.lead: In 1998, MPs who voted as agreed got immunity. Ajit Singh, who abstained, did not.
points: The majority said immunity covers only what is linked to an actual speech or vote in the House.
Ajit Singh did not vote, so the 1998 majority gave him no immunity.
Sita Soren (2024) overruled this: bribery is not protected under Article 105(2).

POL-R21-PRIV-Sita-background.lead: Sita Soren, a JMM MLA in Jharkhand, claimed immunity under Article 194(2).
points: She was accused of taking a bribe for the 2012 Rajya Sabha election but voted for her own party's candidate.
Article 194(2) gives immunity to State legislators. Article 105(2) is the matching rule for MPs.
Article 122 says courts cannot inquire into Parliament's internal procedure. It is not about legislators' immunity.

POL-R21-PRIV-Sita-bench.lead: Sita Soren (4 March 2024): seven judges, unanimous, led by CJI D. Y. Chandrachud.
points: It overruled P. V. Narasimha Rao (1998), which a five-judge bench had decided 3:2.
It held that taking a bribe is a crime the moment the bribe is accepted, whatever the vote cast later.

POL-R21-RES-87th-reservation-census.lead: The 87th Amendment (2003) replaced the 1991 census with the 2001 census for SC/ST seat reservation.

POL-R21-RH-1996-1999-legislative-fates.lead: Each bill lapsed with its own Lok Sabha: 1996 (11th), 1998 (12th). The 1999 bill was the 85th.

1998: the 84th Amendment Bill was introduced in the 12th Lok Sabha and lapsed with it.
1999: the 85th Amendment Bill was introduced in the 13th Lok Sabha. None of these bills became law.

POL-R21-RH-2008-2014-bill-course.lead: The 108th Bill started in Rajya Sabha in 2008, passed it 186:1 in 2010, and lapsed in 2014.
points: It was introduced in Rajya Sabha in May 2008, during the 14th Lok Sabha, and passed there on 9 March 2010.
A bill pending in Lok Sabha lapses when Lok Sabha is dissolved. So it lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha in 2014.
Rajya Sabha is never dissolved. The 128th Bill (2023) became the 106th Amendment.

POL-R21-RH-2023-event-date-match.lead: In September 2023 it was introduced on the 19th, passed by LS on the 20th, RS on the 21st, assent on the 28th.
points: So the answer is 2–4–3–1 (option 1). The law is the 106th Amendment Act, 2023 (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam).

POL-R21-RH-early-extension-titles.lead: Article 334 was extended seven times. The 8th, 23rd and 45th Acts are dated 1959, 1969 and 1980.

False — not while CM's confidence remains

points: If a minister differs with the CM, the CM can ask him to resign or advise his dismissal.

POL-736-LAX-05.lead: The Cabinet is the small senior core of the Council of Ministers.
points: The Council of Ministers is the larger body: Cabinet ministers, ministers of state and deputy ministers.
The Governor is not part of the Cabinet.
It is a political executive body, not a court or civil-service committee.

POL-736-LAX-06.lead: The CM chooses ministers, assigns portfolios and can demand resignations.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: True — Governor appoints on CM's advice

points: The CM's resignation or death dissolves the whole Council of Ministers.

POL-736-LAX-07.lead: As leader of the House, the CM advises on summoning and proroguing sessions.
points: The CM can also recommend dissolution of the Assembly to the Governor.
High Court judges are appointed by the President (Article 217).
The Speaker certifies Money Bills and is removed only by an Assembly resolution.

POL-736-LAX-08.lead: Every Chief Minister is a member of the Inter-State Council.
points: The Inter-State Council is set up under Article 263; the Prime Minister chairs it.
Finance Commission, Election Commission and CAG are independent offices, not held by a CM.
POL-736-LAX-08.also: CMs are also members of NITI Aayog's Governing Council and the Zonal Councils.

POL-736-LAX-09.lead: Ministerial ranks come from convention, not from the Constitution.
points: The Constitution only mentions a 'Council of Ministers' headed by the CM.
Ministers of State are generally not Cabinet members.
Portfolios are allotted by the CM, not fixed by the Constitution.

POL-736-LAX-10.lead: Cabinet committees are of two types: standing and ad hoc.
points: Standing committees are permanent; ad hoc committees are temporary and dissolve after their task.
They are extra-constitutional, set up by the CM as needed.

POL-736-LAX-11.lead: Unlike Britain, India has no rule of ministerial countersignature.
points: In Britain, a minister must countersign the Crown's public acts, creating legal responsibility.
Courts cannot inquire into advice given to the Governor (Article 163(3)).
Ministers act collectively; no individual minister has a veto.

POL-736-LAX-12.lead: A CM with Assembly majority cannot be dismissed at the Governor's whim.
points: Article 164(2) makes the Council responsible to the Assembly; the pleasure clause works within this.
Majority is tested on the floor of the House (S.R. Bommai, 1994).
The Legislative Council and President have no such role.

POL-736-LAX-13.lead: Collective responsibility means the whole ministry resigns, Council members included.
points: Article 164(2): the Council is collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
Ministers from the Legislative Council also go, as they are part of the same ministry.
The Legislative Council cannot pass a no-confidence motion.

POL-736-LAX-14.lead: A ministry that lost confidence cannot bind the Governor to dissolve the Assembly.
points: The Governor may first see if another leader can form a stable government.
The Speaker and Legislative Council have no say in dissolution.

POL-736-LAX-15.lead: The CM's resignation or death automatically dissolves the Council of Ministers.
points: Any other minister's exit only creates a vacancy.
The Assembly is not dissolved automatically; the Governor never becomes CM.

POL-736-LAX-16.lead: Shamsher Singh (1974): Governor acts on ministers' aid and advice.
points: The case held the President and Governor are formal heads; real power lies with ministers.
Only genuine discretionary matters are an exception.

POL-736-LAX-17.lead: Cabinet committees also take decisions; the Cabinet can review them.
points: They sort out issues and frame proposals for the Cabinet.
They are executive bodies, not judicial; no legislative ratification is needed.

POL-736-LAX-18.lead: The State Cabinet performs all four roles listed.
points: It is also the chief executive authority and deals with major appointments.

POL-736-LAX-19.lead: 94th Amendment (2006) freed Bihar; added Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.
points: Article 164(1) requires a tribal welfare minister in these States.
Present list: Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha.
Bihar was dropped because most tribal areas went to Jharkhand in 2000.

POL-736-LAX-20.lead: Article 163: Governor uses discretion only where the Constitution requires it.
points: Aid and advice is the general rule.
Policy disagreement or a Legislative Council request gives no discretion.
Under Article 163(2), the Governor's decision on what is discretionary is final.

POL-736-LAX-21.lead: Article 167 places both duties on the Chief Minister.
POL-736-LAX-21.also: Article 167(c): Governor can ask that a single minister's decision be placed before the Council.

POL-736-LAX-22.lead: Article 167(c): CM must place such a matter before the Council.
points: This applies to a minister's decision not yet considered by the Council.
No High Court approval, Legislative Council ratification or automatic loss of office follows.

POL-736-P342-01.lead: Article 163(1): the Chief Minister heads the Council of Ministers.
points: The Speaker presides over the Assembly.
The Chief Secretary is the top civil servant.
The Advocate General is the State's chief law officer (Article 165).

POL-736-P342-02.lead: Article 163(3): courts cannot ask whether or what advice was given.
points: It does not shield every Governor's action from judicial review.
Ministers' qualifications and Assembly proceedings are not covered by this clause.

POL-736-P342-03.lead: Article 164(1): Governor appoints other ministers on the CM's advice.
points: The Governor appoints the Chief Minister.
The President, the Assembly and the High Court have no role here.

POL-736-P343-01.lead: Article 167(c): CM must place the minister's decision before the Council.

POL-736-P344-01.lead: Article 164(2): collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.
points: This holds even in States with a Legislative Council.
Ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure, but responsibility is to the Assembly.

POL-736-P344-02.lead: Article 164(4): non-member minister loses office after six consecutive months.
points: He must become a member of either House of the State Legislature within that time.
Nothing happens automatically to the Assembly, and he cannot continue to the next election.

POL-736-P344-03.lead: Ministry: maximum 15% of Assembly strength, minimum 12 including CM.
points: Article 164(1A) was added by the 91st Amendment, 2003.
Only Legislative Assembly strength counts, not both Houses.
10% and 'no minimum' or 'exactly 15' are not the rule.

POL-736-P345-01.lead: Article 164(1B): defection-disqualified member cannot become a minister.
points: The bar lasts till his term ends or he is re-elected, whichever is earlier.
Added by the 91st Amendment, 2003.
The Constitution says nothing about Deputy CMs.

POL-736-P346-02.lead: Article 166 is about form and authentication, not personal decisions.
points: Article 166(3): Governor makes rules for convenient transaction of business.

POL-736-P346-03.lead: Article 177: a minister may speak in the other House but not vote.
points: Every minister and the Advocate General can speak and take part in both Houses.
There is no Money Bill exception for voting.

POL-E44-CUR-736-001.lead: The CM leads the Council and coordinates the whole government.
points: The CM gives direction; he does not merely record decisions.
Departmental ministers run portfolios; overall coordination is the CM's job.
The Chief Secretary heads the civil service; political direction is the CM's.

LX-PQ-073.lead: Both are true; R is about Parliament's law, not court's power.

Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Parliament may regulate elections by law

points: A's power comes from the Constitution itself, so R does not explain A.
LX-PQ-073.also: Parliament made the Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952.

LX-PQ-096.lead: District judges are under the High Court's control (Article 235).
points: The Governor appoints district judges in consultation with the High Court (Article 233).
Posting, promotion and leave are controlled by the High Court.
The Collector and Law Minister have no control.

LX-PQ-166.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are wrong; 2 and 4 are right.

LX-UPSC-2014-Q13.lead: Article 124(1): Parliament can increase Supreme Court judges by law.
points: Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 2019 raised it to 34 including CJI.
The President appoints judges but cannot change their number.

LX-UPSC-2021-Q02.lead: Both points show India differs from Britain's sovereign Parliament.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: True — Constitution and judicial review limit it
True — Article 145(3), five or more judges

points: Britain has no written constitution; its courts cannot strike down Acts of Parliament.

LX-UPSC-2022-Q01.lead: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; contempt is defined by the 1971 Act.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: True — committee (1961, report 1963) led to 1971 Act
False — Contempt of Courts Act defines

POL-741-AT-acting-cji.lead: Article 126: President appoints another Supreme Court judge as acting CJI.
points: No automatic takeover by the senior-most judge without appointment.
A High Court judge can sit only as an ad hoc judge under Article 127.
Judges do not elect an acting CJI.

POL-741-AT-adhoc-conditions.lead: All three conditions apply to ad hoc judges under Article 127.
points: The CJI makes the request; the judge must be qualified for Supreme Court appointment.

POL-741-AT-adhoc-priority.lead: Article 127(2): Supreme Court attendance takes priority over other duties.
points: During attendance the judge has all Supreme Court powers and privileges.
Attendance is a duty, not optional.

POL-741-AT-administrative-charge.lead: Article 146(3) charges SC administrative expenses on the Consolidated Fund of India.
points: These include salaries, allowances and pensions of court staff and officers.
Charged expenditure is not voted by Parliament, so option 3 is wrong.
The charge is on the Union's fund, not every State's fund.
Fees and other money taken by the Court form part of that Consolidated Fund, not the CJI's property.
POL-741-AT-administrative-charge.also: Judges' salaries are also charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 125).

POL-741-AT-advisory-two-classes.lead: Under Article 143(1) the Court 'may' report; under 143(2) it 'shall' report.

head: Clause
Matter
Court's duty
rows: Any question of law or fact of public importance
Disputes under proviso to Article 131 (pre-1950 treaties etc.)

points: Neither clause deals with private or criminal appeals.
Advisory opinions are not binding decrees on the President.
POL-741-AT-advisory-two-classes.also: The reference on Ram Janmabhoomi (made 1993) was returned unanswered by the Court in 1994 (Ismail Faruqui case).

POL-741-AT-age-determination-law.lead: Article 124(2A): Parliament may by law fix the authority and manner for age determination.
points: Clause (2A) was added by the 15th Amendment, 1963.
Governors and State Legislatures have no role over Supreme Court judges.
The CJI cannot settle this by a personal direction; the Article requires a law of Parliament.

POL-741-AT-aid-authorities.lead: Article 144: all civil and judicial authorities in India must act in aid of the Supreme Court.
points: It covers Union and State authorities alike, not only Union ministries.
It is not limited to High Court judges or to Article 143 references.
It backs up Article 142, under which SC decrees are enforceable throughout India.

POL-741-AT-appointment-authority.lead: The President appoints SC judges by warrant under his hand and seal (Article 124(2)).
points: The President acts after consultation with the CJI and other judges as he deems necessary.
In practice the collegium recommends names; the CJI does not appoint alone.
The Speaker and Law Minister have no appointing power.
POL-741-AT-appointment-authority.also: The NJAC (99th Amendment) was struck down in 2015, restoring the collegium.

POL-741-AT-civil-appeal-certificate.lead: Article 133(1) needs both findings in the High Court's certificate under Article 134A.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Substantial question of law of general importance
HC thinks SC must decide it

POL-741-AT-civil-appeal-certificate.also: The valuation test (Rs 20,000) was removed by the 30th Amendment, 1972.

POL-741-AT-common-question-withdrawal.lead: Article 139A(1) lets the SC withdraw such cases and dispose of them itself.
points: The Court may also return the cases to the High Courts after deciding the questions of law.
No State consent is needed; the SC acts on its own motion or on application by the Attorney-General or a party.
It does not quash the cases without deciding the questions.
POL-741-AT-common-question-withdrawal.also: Article 139A was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

POL-741-AT-constitutional-appeal.lead: Article 132 covers civil, criminal or other proceedings with a certificate under Article 134A.
points: The test is a substantial question of law on interpreting the Constitution.
Criminal proceedings are expressly included, so option 1 is wrong.
A death sentence is a separate Article 134 route; no presidential reference is needed.

POL-741-AT-constitutional-location.lead: Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147) deals with the Union judiciary.

POL-741-AT-curative-boundary.lead: A curative petition is not a second appeal; it is rare and strictly limited.
points: It was created in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002).
Grounds are narrow, such as violation of natural justice or judge bias.
A senior advocate must certify it, and it goes first to the three senior-most judges plus the judges who decided.
POL-741-AT-curative-boundary.also: It is a Supreme Court remedy, not a High Court or presidential one.

POL-741-AT-enlargement-agreement.lead: Article 138(2) also needs a law of Parliament for the extra jurisdiction to work.
points: The special agreement between the Government of India and a State is only the first step.
Parliament must then provide by law for the Court to exercise that jurisdiction.
No constitutional amendment or Governor's approval is involved.

POL-741-AT-family-appeal-boundary.lead: Only a contested final judgment is appealable; consent decrees and interlocutory orders are not.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: True — appeal lies to HC, s.19(1)

points: The appeal must be filed within 30 days and is heard by a Bench of two or more HC judges.

POL-741-AT-family-establishment.lead: Section 3: State sets up Family Courts after consulting the High Court; mandatory above one million population.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: State acts after consulting High Court
Mandatory where city population exceeds 10 lakh

points: For other areas, the State may set up Family Courts as it deems necessary.

POL-741-AT-family-representation.lead: Section 13: no party is entitled as of right to a lawyer; court may appoint amicus curiae.
points: Parties usually appear in person to keep proceedings informal.
The court may still seek a legal expert's help as amicus curiae in the interest of justice.
So 'unconditional right' and 'only advocates may appear' are both wrong.

POL-741-AT-family-settlement.lead: Section 9 asks the Family Court to try to persuade parties to settle, where suitable.
points: The court acts consistently with the nature and circumstances of the case.
It cannot force a settlement; parties' consent is needed.
If settlement fails, the court hears and decides the case; there is no automatic Lok Adalat transfer.

POL-741-AT-gram-appeal-routes.lead: Criminal appeals go to the Court of Session; civil appeals go to the District Court.
points: Criminal appeals are under section 33 of the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008.
Civil appeals are under section 34.
Gram Sabhas and Collectors are not appellate forums.

POL-741-AT-gram-appointment.lead: State Government appoints the Nyayadhikari in consultation with the High Court.
points: The person must be eligible to be appointed a Judicial Magistrate of the first class.
Nyayadhikaris are judicial officers, not elected sarpanchs or revenue officers.

POL-741-AT-gram-commencement.lead: The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 came into force on 2 October 2009.
points: The date marks Gandhi Jayanti.
The Act was passed in 2008 but enforced the next year.
It sets up courts at the intermediate panchayat level for quick, cheap justice.

POL-741-AT-gram-mobile-scope.lead: Gram Nyayalayas are mobile courts with both civil and criminal jurisdiction.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Can hold mobile court near parties
True — as given in the Act's Schedules

points: Headquarters is at the intermediate panchayat level.

POL-741-AT-inauguration.lead: The Supreme Court was inaugurated on 28 January 1950.
points: It began two days after the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.
It first sat in the Chamber of Princes in the Parliament building.
26 November 1949 is when the Constitution was adopted.
POL-741-AT-inauguration.also: It replaced the Federal Court of India (1937) and the Privy Council's appellate role.

POL-741-AT-inquiry-committee.lead: The committee has an SC judge (or CJI), an HC Chief Justice and a distinguished jurist.
points: The Speaker or Rajya Sabha Chairman constitutes it after admitting the motion.
It does not contain MPs, the Law Minister or the Attorney-General.
It is not made of the CJI and two senior judges.

POL-741-AT-inquiry-notice.lead: A removal motion needs 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members' signatures.
points: This is under section 3(1) of the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.
The Speaker or Chairman may admit or refuse the motion.
Final removal needs a special majority in each House, then the President's order.

POL-741-AT-integrated-hierarchy.lead: One court hierarchy enforces both Union and State laws in India.
points: The Supreme Court is at the top, then High Courts, then subordinate courts.
This differs from the USA, which has separate federal and state courts.
Subordinate judges are appointed by Governors/High Courts, not the Supreme Court.
POL-741-AT-integrated-hierarchy.also: The Government of India Act, 1935 shaped this single integrated system.

POL-741-AT-no-minimum-age.lead: The Constitution prescribes no minimum age for Supreme Court judges.
points: Article 124(3) needs Indian citizenship plus HC judge (5 yrs), HC advocate (10 yrs) or distinguished jurist.
35 years is the President's minimum age, not a judge's.
Only the upper limit (retire at 65) is fixed.

POL-741-AT-oath-authority.lead: Oath is taken before the President or his appointee, in the Third Schedule form.
points: This is under Article 124(6).
The Third Schedule holds oath forms; the Fourth allots Rajya Sabha seats.
The CJI, Speaker and Prime Minister do not administer this oath.

POL-741-AT-open-majority-dissent.lead: Article 145 requires open-court judgments and allows majority decisions with dissents.
points: Advisory opinions under Article 143 are also delivered in open court.

POL-741-AT-original-private-party.lead: Article 131 covers only disputes between the Union and States or among States.
points: A private party cannot invoke Article 131 even if the Union is a defendant.
The dispute must involve a question on which a legal right depends.
The company must sue in an ordinary civil court instead.

POL-741-AT-parliament-conduct.lead: Article 121 allows discussion only on a motion for an address praying for removal.
points: Otherwise Parliament cannot discuss an SC or HC judge's conduct in duties.
Question hour, budget debates and ministers' requests are not exceptions.
Article 211 bars State Legislatures from discussing such conduct at all.

POL-741-AT-postretirement-practice.lead: Article 124(7) bars a retired SC judge from pleading before any court or authority in India.
points: The bar covers tribunals anywhere in India, not only in Delhi.
There is no waiting period after which it lifts.
Retired judges may still take up arbitration, commissions or tribunal posts.
POL-741-AT-postretirement-practice.also: Retired High Court judges may plead in the Supreme Court and other High Courts (Article 220).

POL-741-AT-removal-grounds.lead: Only proved misbehaviour or incapacity can be a ground for removal.
points: Removal needs an address by both Houses with a special majority, then the President's order.
Unpopularity or loss of Cabinet confidence is not a ground.
No SC judge has been removed so far.

POL-741-AT-retired-attendance.lead: Under Article 128, the CJI asks with President's previous consent and the retired judge's consent.
points: The retired judge cannot be forced to sit.
Such a judge gets allowances set by the President but is not deemed a regular judge.
No election by Parliament is involved.

POL-741-AT-rules-approval.lead: The Supreme Court makes rules with the President's approval, subject to parliamentary law.
points: These rules regulate practice and procedure, under Article 145(1).
They cannot override a law made by Parliament.
Governors and the Speaker have no role.

POL-741-AT-seat.lead: Under Article 130, the CJI chooses another seat with the President's approval.
points: Delhi is the normal seat of the Supreme Court.
No State Assembly, Governor or Cabinet decides this alone.

POL-741-AT-specialleave-character.lead: Article 136 is a wide discretionary power, not an appeal as of right.
points: It covers any judgment, decree, order or sentence of any court or tribunal.
It is not limited to final High Court civil judgments.
Military courts and tribunals are excluded.

POL-741-AT-staff-appointment.lead: Article 146(1): the CJI, or a judge or officer he directs, appoints SC staff.
points: The proviso lets the President require UPSC consultation for specified posts.
The Law Minister and Attorney-General have no appointing role.

POL-741-AT-staff-financial-rules.lead: Rules on salaries, allowances, leave or pensions need the President's approval.
points: This is the proviso to Article 146(2).
Other conditions of service are set by rules made by the CJI, subject to parliamentary law.

POL-741-AT-tenure-resignation.lead: An SC judge retires at 65 and resigns by writing to the President.
points: Retirement age is in Article 124(2).
High Court judges retire at 62.
Resignation is addressed to the President, not the CJI or Governor.

POL-741-AT-union-list-enlargement.lead: Article 138(1) lets Parliament by law enlarge SC jurisdiction on Union List matters.
points: States cannot do this by executive order.
Article 143 is only for advisory opinions.
Article 138(2) is the separate route through a Union–State special agreement.

POL-741-CH-01.lead: Presidential requests for opinions invoke advisory jurisdiction under Article 143.

POL-741-CH-02.lead: Article 145(3) requires at least five judges for substantial constitutional questions.
points: Such a bench is called a Constitution Bench.
The same minimum applies to hearing an Article 143 reference.
Larger benches (7, 9, 13) are used when earlier rulings need review.
POL-741-CH-02.also: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) was heard by 13 judges, the largest bench so far.

POL-741-HIST-adm-khanna-dissent.lead: Justice H. R. Khanna alone held that liberty survives an Emergency.
points: The 4–1 majority (Ray, Beg, Chandrachud, Bhagwati) held habeas corpus petitions not maintainable during the 1975 Emergency.
A. N. Ray was the Chief Justice heading the majority bench.
M. H. Beg and Y. V. Chandrachud both joined the majority.
POL-741-HIST-adm-khanna-dissent.also: Puttaswamy (2017) declared the ADM Jabalpur majority view overruled.

POL-741-HIST-statutory-origin-constituti.lead: The Supreme Court legally came into being when the Constitution began: 26 January 1950.

points: The Court first sat two days later, on 28 January 1950, in the Chamber of Princes, Parliament House.
The original Constitution provided 8 judges (CJI + 7).

So the A–B–C order is 26–31–34, option 4.

POL-741-HIST-supersession-pairs.lead: 1973: Ray superseded three judges; 1977: Beg superseded Khanna.
points: Options 1 and 3 swap the names or years; option 4 wrongly names Chandrachud for 1977.
Khanna was superseded soon after his ADM Jabalpur dissent; he resigned.
POL-741-HIST-supersession-pairs.also: The 1973 supersession followed the Kesavananda Bharati judgment.

POL-741-P286-01.lead: Article 124(1) sets up the Court: a CJI and other judges.

POL-741-P290-01.lead: Article 124(3) lists all three as alternative qualifications for a citizen.
points: Any one of the three is enough; Indian citizenship is a must in every case.

POL-741-P291-01.lead: Removal needs a special majority in each House in the same session.
points: Each House: majority of total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting.
Simple majority is too low; unanimity and 'two-thirds of total membership' are not the rule.
The address is then presented to the President, who orders removal.

POL-741-P293-01.lead: Article 131 gives the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction in Centre–State disputes.

POL-741-P294-01.lead: Article 136(2) excludes Armed Forces tribunals from special leave.
points: Special leave can be granted against any court or tribunal in India, except those under Armed Forces laws.
High Courts, civil courts and consumer commissions are all covered by Article 136.

POL-741-P295-01.lead: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right to approach the Supreme Court.
points: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

POL-741-P295-02.lead: Article 129: Supreme Court is a court of record and can punish contempt.

Article
Subject
