points: Article 215 gives the same status to High Courts.

POL-741-P296-01.lead: Article 137 lets the Supreme Court review its own judgments.

POL-741-PROC-cji-recommendation-route.lead: Law Minister forwards to the PM, who advises the President.
points: Under the Memorandum of Procedure, the Law Minister seeks the outgoing CJI's recommendation.
The Law Minister puts it to the Prime Minister, who advises the President to appoint.
Only the President appoints judges (Article 124(2)); the other options reverse roles.

POL-741-REM-adhoc-eligibility-powers.lead: Article 127 requires SC qualification and gives full SC powers while attending.
points: Ad hoc judges are used when quorum of permanent judges is lacking; CJI acts with President's consent after consulting the HC Chief Justice.

POL-741-REM-advisory-five.lead: Article 145(3) requires at least five judges for Article 143 references.
points: The same five-judge minimum applies to cases involving a substantial question of constitutional interpretation.
Two, three or seven are not the constitutional minimum.

POL-741-REM-citizenship.lead: Citizenship is mandatory for every Supreme Court appointee under Article 124(3).
points: The jurist route only replaces the judicial or bar experience requirement, not citizenship.
Residence does not substitute, and a later oath cannot cure missing eligibility.

POL-741-REM-composition.lead: Article 124(1): CJI plus other judges; Parliament may increase the number by law.
points: The original figure was CJI + 7, but Parliament has enlarged it several times.
The number is set by an Act of Parliament, not by executive order.
High Court Chief Justices are not ex officio members of the Supreme Court.

POL-741-REM-judges-residuals.lead: Both statements correctly describe the Second (1993) and Third (1998) Judges Cases.
points: The Third Judges Case widened the collegium to CJI plus four senior-most judges.

POL-741-REM-oath-faith.lead: The Third Schedule oath includes true faith and allegiance to the Constitution.
points: Judges also swear to uphold the Constitution and the laws.
The oath never places government policy above the Constitution or bars judicial review.
Judgments are public once delivered; no secrecy undertaking about them exists.

POL-741-REM-removal-order.lead: Under Article 124(4), the President's order removes the judge.
points: Presiding officers only transmit the address; they cannot remove a judge.
The inquiry committee under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 only reports findings.
The CJI has no power to remove a Supreme Court judge.

POL-741-REM-retired-sitting-status.lead: Article 128: full SC powers while sitting, but not otherwise deemed a judge.
points: The CJI may request a retired judge to sit with the President's previous consent.
Powers are judicial, not merely advisory, and need no delegation from any minister.
Permanent membership is not restored by the request.

POL-741-REM-state-discussion.lead: Article 211 bars State Legislatures from discussing any SC or HC judge's judicial conduct.
points: Article 121 (Parliament) allows discussion on a removal motion; Article 211 has no such exception.
This is because only Parliament can remove judges.
No Governor consent lifts the bar, and it covers SC and HC judges.

POL-741-SUPP-aor-filing-and-appearance.lead: Under the Supreme Court Rules, only an AoR files; others plead when instructed.

POL-741-SUPP-apex-replacement.lead: The Supreme Court replaced the Federal Court and the Privy Council.
points: Federal Court (1937) was India's top court under the 1935 Act.
Privy Council appeals were ended by the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949.
High Courts, Election Commission and PSCs continue to exist separately.

POL-741-SUPP-building-architect.lead: Ganesh Bhikaji Deolalikar, first Indian head of CPWD, designed it.
points: The Court moved into this building on Tilak Marg in 1958.
Lutyens and Baker designed Rashtrapati Bhavan and Parliament House; Le Corbusier planned Chandigarh.

POL-741-SUPP-cji-seniority-fitness.lead: By convention, the senior-most Supreme Court judge considered fit becomes CJI.
points: The MoP says the senior-most judge considered fit to hold office should be appointed.
There is no election; HC Chief Justices are not automatically made CJI.

POL-741-SUPP-contempt-classification.lead: Breach of undertaking is civil contempt; prejudicing proceedings is criminal contempt.

POL-741-SUPP-court-record-evidence.lead: Court-of-record records are preserved and carry authoritative evidentiary value.
points: Its records cannot be questioned when produced before any court.
Budgets, cause lists or abolition of appeals have nothing to do with this status.

POL-741-SUPP-criminal-appeal-1970.lead: The 1970 Act gives appeal as of right for life or ten-plus years.
points: Article 134(1) covers death sentences; Article 134(2) lets Parliament widen this.
The Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970 covers reversal of acquittal with life or at least 10 years.

POL-741-SUPP-fair-criticism-final-case.lead: Section 5 protects fair comment on a case heard and finally decided.
points: Wilful disobedience of a court order is civil contempt.
Threatening a witness interferes with justice, which is criminal contempt.
Publications about pending cases are protected only in limited situations, not always.

POL-741-SUPP-family-gram-act-years.lead: Family Courts Act is 1984; Gram Nyayalayas Act is 2008.
points: Gram Nyayalayas came into force on 2 October 2009.
1987 is the year of the Legal Services Authorities Act.

POL-741-SUPP-fathima-supreme-service.lead: Fathima Beevi, first woman SC judge, served from 1989 to 1992.
points: She was appointed in October 1989 and retired in April 1992.
She later became Governor of Tamil Nadu (1997–2001).

POL-741-SUPP-financial-emergency-directi.lead: Article 360(4)(b) allows cutting salaries of Supreme Court and High Court judges.
points: The President, not a Governor, issues such directions.
Judges are expressly included, not exempt, during a Financial Emergency.

POL-741-SUPP-first-two-chief-justices.lead: Harilal Kania was the first CJI (1950–51); Patanjali Sastri was second.
points: Option 1 reverses the order.
S. R. Das and Mehr Chand Mahajan came later; Y. V. Chandrachud was the 16th CJI.
POL-741-SUPP-first-two-chief-justices.also: Y. V. Chandrachud had the longest tenure as CJI (1978–85).

POL-741-SUPP-gram-natural-justice.lead: Section 30 asks Gram Nyayalayas to follow natural justice principles.
points: They are not strictly bound by the Evidence Act rules.
Executive pleasure, party discipline or police instructions are not guiding principles of any court.

POL-741-SUPP-judges-cases-principles.lead: First: no concurrence; Second: CJI primacy; Third: CJI + four senior-most.
points: So the order is 2–3–1, option 4.

POL-741-SUPP-legislative-irregularity-il.lead: Courts cannot probe mere irregularity but can check illegality or unconstitutionality.
points: Articles 122 and 212 bar challenges only on 'irregularity of procedure'.
Raja Ram Pal (2007) held substantive illegality is open to judicial review.
Privilege never overrides the Constitution.

POL-741-SUPP-notice-admission-discretion.lead: The Speaker may admit or refuse the motion after consultation.
points: Section 3, Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968: 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members must sign.
Signatures only start the process; the Election Commission has no role.

POL-741-SUPP-oath-duties.lead: The oath covers sovereignty and impartial duty, never party loyalty.

POL-741-SUPP-ordinary-bench-two.lead: Supreme Court Rules, 2013: cases are heard by a Bench of at least two judges.
points: Order VI rule 1 says every cause goes before a Bench of not less than two judges.
Some listed matters (e.g., certain interlocutory or chamber matters) may be heard by a single judge.
Five judges is the minimum only for constitutional questions and Article 143 references (Art 145(3)).
POL-741-SUPP-ordinary-bench-two.also: Art 145(3): substantial question of constitutional interpretation needs at least five judges.

POL-741-SUPP-original-eight.lead: Originally: 1 Chief Justice + 7 other judges = 8 judges in total.
points: Article 124(1) originally fixed one CJI and not more than seven other judges.
7 is only the other judges, not the total.
Parliament can raise the number by law; it is now 34 (CJI + 33) since 2019.
POL-741-SUPP-original-eight.also: Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2019 raised strength to 34.

POL-741-SUPP-preconstitution-federal-exc.lead: Article 143(2) lets the President refer disputes excluded by Article 131's proviso.

head: No.
Option
Why
rows: Special leave; never an appeal as of right

points: Article 131's proviso keeps disputes from pre-Constitution treaties, agreements, sanads etc. out of original jurisdiction.
Under 143(2), the Supreme Court must give its opinion on such a reference.
POL-741-SUPP-preconstitution-federal-exc.also: Under 143(1) the Court may refuse an opinion; under 143(2) it must give one.

POL-741-SUPP-retired-judge-allowances.lead: Article 128: the President decides the allowances by order.
points: The retired judge sits only with the President's previous consent and the judge's own consent.
The CJI makes the request.
While sitting, the judge has SC powers and privileges but is not otherwise deemed an SC judge.

POL-741-SUPP-review-thirty-days.lead: A Supreme Court review petition must be filed within 30 days.
points: Order XLVII rule 2, Supreme Court Rules 2013: 30 days from the judgment or order.
Review power comes from Article 137.
Review petitions are normally decided by circulation, without oral hearing.
POL-741-SUPP-review-thirty-days.also: Special leave petitions have different limitation periods (e.g., 90 days in civil matters).

POL-741-SUPP-senior-advocate-designation.lead: Only the Supreme Court or a High Court can designate senior advocates.
points: Section 16(2): designation needs the advocate's consent.
The court must be of opinion that ability, standing at the Bar or special knowledge deserves it.
Collector, Law Minister or Panchayat have no such role.
POL-741-SUPP-senior-advocate-designation.also: Indira Jaising case (2017) laid down guidelines for senior designation.

POL-741-SUPP-state-psc-reference.lead: The President alone refers misbehaviour of any PSC member to the Supreme Court.
points: Art 317(1): removal for misbehaviour only by President's order after a Supreme Court inquiry.
This applies even to State PSC members, though the Governor appoints them.
The Governor may only suspend the member pending the inquiry (Art 317(2)).
POL-741-SUPP-state-psc-reference.also: State PSC members are appointed by the Governor but removable only by the President.

PRAC-POL-D84E97734BE0.lead: All legitimate government payments come out of the CFI; SC receipts go to Public Account.
points: Article 284: suitors' deposits and other money received by courts go to the Public Account of India.
PRAC-POL-D84E97734BE0.also: Art 266 creates the Consolidated Fund and the Public Account.

LX-PQ-142.lead: Article 217(3): President decides a HC judge's age after consulting the CJI.
points: The President's decision on the age question is final.
Neither the HC Chief Justice, the Governor nor the Attorney-General is consulted under this clause.
Added by the 15th Amendment, 1963.

LX-PQ-190.lead: Reservation is under Article 200, is discretionary, and compulsory if HC is endangered.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — Governor may reserve at discretion

points: Article 201 then deals with what the President does with a reserved bill.

POL-742-CH-01.lead: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs 'for any other purpose' too.

head: No.
Option
Why
rows: Special leave to appeal to SC
FRs and any other legal right

POL-742-CH-01.also: Art 32 is itself a fundamental right; Art 226 is not.

POL-742-CH-02.lead: Article 235 gives High Courts control over district and subordinate courts.
points: Control covers postings, promotions and leave of judicial officers below district judge.
Andhra State High Court started at Guntur on 5 July 1954.
Separate AP High Court began on 1 January 2019, first sitting from temporary premises in Vijayawada.
POL-742-HC-PRACTICE-01.also: The 2014 common court was the High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad for Telangana and AP.

POL-742-HC-PRACTICE-02.lead: Even a competent High Court may decline, giving reasons, on forum conveniens grounds.
points: Art 226(2) lets any HC where part of the cause of action arose hear the case.
Having jurisdiction does not force the court to decide merits; writ relief is discretionary.
Kusum Ingots (2004) recognised this forum conveniens principle.
Neither withdrawal by the petitioner nor the respondent's head office decides it.

POL-742-HC-PRACTICE-03.lead: Section 100 CPC: second appeal only on a substantial question of law, formulated by court.
points: Section 100(1): second appeal lies only if a substantial question of law is involved.
Section 100(4): the High Court must formulate that question itself.
A second appeal is not a rehearing of facts like a first appeal.
Supreme Court certification is not needed.

POL-742-HC-PRACTICE-04.lead: Both addresses must be presented to the President in the same session.
points: Art 124(4) needs a special majority in each House and presentation in the same session.
Art 217(1)(b) applies this removal method to High Court judges.
Votes cannot cure the timing defect; State Legislature, CJI or President cannot waive it.

POL-742-P312-01.lead: Article 231 lets Parliament set up a common High Court for two or more States.

head: No.
Option
Why
rows: A High Court for each State

POL-742-P312-01.also: Example: Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh share one High Court.

POL-742-P312-02.lead: Article 214: there shall be a High Court for each State.
points: Article 231 is the exception allowing a common High Court.

POL-742-P313-01.lead: Article 216: the President decides how many judges each High Court needs.
points: Unlike the Supreme Court, Parliament does not fix High Court strength.
Strength therefore differs from one High Court to another.
Governor and CJI have no power to fix numbers.

POL-742-P313-02.lead: The Chief Minister is not named in Article 217(1) consultation.
points: In practice the Governor acts on ministerial advice, but the text names only the Governor.

POL-742-P313-03.lead: Article 217(2): ten years in judicial office or as HC advocate qualifies.
points: Indian citizenship is also required.

POL-742-P313-04.lead: No minimum age and no 'distinguished jurist' route exist for HC judges.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — exists only for SC, Art 124(3)

POL-742-P314-01.lead: High Court judges retire at 62; Supreme Court judges at 65.
points: Age was raised from 60 to 62 by the 15th Amendment, 1963.
65 applies to Supreme Court judges under Art 124(2).

POL-742-P314-02.lead: Art 217(3): President decides after consulting the CJI; decision is final.
points: Governor, HC Chief Justice and Parliament have no role here.
Clause added by the 15th Amendment, 1963.

POL-742-P314-03.lead: Article 221(1): Parliament fixes High Court judges' salaries by law.
points: Salaries are charged on the State Consolidated Fund, but the State does not fix them.
Pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Salaries cannot be cut to their disadvantage after appointment, except in financial emergency.
POL-742-P314-03.also: High Court Judges (Salaries and Conditions of Service) Act, 1954.

POL-742-P314-04.lead: Charged expenditure is not voted on, but the legislature may discuss it.
points: Art 203(1): estimates of charged expenditure are not submitted to vote.
The same clause says nothing prevents discussion of them.
The Governor cannot turn a charged item into a voted one.
POL-742-P314-04.also: Art 113(1) is the matching rule for Parliament.

POL-742-P315-01.lead: Article 222: President transfers HC judges after consulting the CJI.
points: The Prime Minister, Law Minister or destination Governor are not named.
Second Judges case (1993): CJI must consult senior-most SC judges (collegium).

POL-742-P315-02.lead: A High Court judge resigns by writing addressed to the President.
points: Art 217(1)(a) proviso: signed writing to the President.
The Governor only administers the oath (Art 219).
Resignation is separate from removal by Parliament.

POL-742-P315-03.lead: Art 223: President appoints another judge of that HC as acting Chief Justice.
points: Applies when the office is vacant or the Chief Justice is absent or unable to act.
Advocate General, civil servants and district judges are not eligible under this Article.

POL-742-P315-04.lead: Article 224(1) allows additional judges for temporary work, up to two years.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Temporary rise in work or arrears

points: The President appoints them; they must hold HC judge qualifications.

POL-742-P315-05.lead: Art 224(2): acting judge serves until the permanent judge resumes duty.
points: The age limit of 62 under Art 224(3) still applies.
The two-year ceiling is for additional judges only.
The President appoints, not the Governor.

POL-742-P315-06.lead: Art 224(3): no additional or acting judge can hold office beyond 62.
points: An unexpired appointment order cannot override the constitutional age limit.
The State cabinet has no power to extend it.

POL-742-P315-07.lead: Article 224A needs both the President's consent and the retired judge's consent.
points: The HC Chief Justice makes the request, with the President's previous consent.
No retired judge can be required to sit against his will.
Allowances are fixed by the President.
POL-742-P315-07.also: Article 224A was added by the 15th Amendment, 1963.

POL-742-P315-08.lead: A recalled judge has full HC powers while sitting, but is not otherwise a judge.
points: Art 224A: jurisdiction, powers and privileges of an HC judge while so sitting.
He is not deemed a High Court judge for other purposes.
It is not advisory and not a permanent reappointment.

POL-742-P316-01.lead: Article 215 makes every High Court a court of record with contempt power.

head: No.
Option
Why
rows: High Court as court of record

POL-742-P317-01.lead: Art 227(4) excludes Armed Forces courts and tribunals from HC superintendence.
points: District courts, civil courts and revenue tribunals in its territory are all covered.
Superintendence is both administrative and judicial.

POL-742-P317-02.lead: HCs can call for returns, but their rules must obey law and need Governor's approval.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Rules may ignore law, no approval

POL-742-P318-01.lead: Chief Justice appoints HC staff; pay and pension rules need Governor's approval.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Pay, leave, pension rules need Governor

points: Administrative expenses of the HC are charged on the State Consolidated Fund (Art 229(3)).

POL-742-P319-01.lead: Art 348(2) allows Hindi/State language in HC proceedings, but not judgments.
points: Official Languages Act 1963, s.7, separately allows such language for judgments, with an English translation.

POL-742-SUPP-constitutional-location.lead: High Courts are in Part VI, Articles 214 to 231.

POL-742-SUPP-hc-appointment-two-sc-colle.lead: For HC appointments, the CJI consults two senior-most SC judges.
points: Three or five wrongly add the CJI to the count of colleagues.
POL-742-SUPP-hc-appointment-two-sc-colle.also: Third Judges Case: In re Special Reference 1 of 1998.

POL-742-SUPP-hc-composition-positive.lead: Art 216: a Chief Justice plus judges the President deems necessary.
points: Option 1 is wrong: other HC judges are full judges, not subordinate officers.
Option 3 is wrong: the Constitution fixes no number; the President decides strength.
Option 4 is wrong: district judges are not ex officio HC judges.

POL-742-SUPP-hc-transfer-consultation.lead: HC transfers: CJI plus four senior-most SC judges, and both HC Chief Justices.
points: Two SC judges is the rule for HC appointments, not transfers.

POL-742-SUPP-retirement-fifteenth-amendm.lead: The 15th Amendment, 1963 raised HC judges' retirement age to 62.
POL-742-SUPP-retirement-fifteenth-amendm.also: The 114th Amendment Bill (2010) to raise it to 65 lapsed; it is still 62.

POL-742-SUPP-supervisory-rules-forms-fee.lead: Art 227 lets the High Court make rules, forms and fee tables.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Rules and forms for subordinate courts

points: Such rules must not clash with existing law and need the Governor's prior approval.

POL-742-SUPP-ut-jurisdiction-230.lead: Art 230: Parliament by law extends or excludes HC jurisdiction over a UT.

head: No.
Article
Subject
rows: Common HC for two or more States

points: A State Assembly or Governor cannot alter HC jurisdiction over a UT.

LX-PQ-091.lead: Art 233: the Governor appoints district judges, consulting the High Court.
points: The High Court is consulted but does not appoint.
The State PSC and CM have no appointing role for district judges.
LX-PQ-091.also: Other subordinate judges: Governor appoints after consulting State PSC and High Court (Art 234).

POL-743-A01.lead: Subordinate courts: Part VI, Chapter VI, Articles 233–237.

POL-743-A02.lead: Direct recruits need seven years' practice and High Court recommendation.
points: Art 233(2): a person not in government service must be an advocate or pleader for at least seven years.
He must also be recommended by the High Court; six years with no recommendation fails both.
The State PSC has no role here, and the Governor cannot waive these conditions.

POL-743-A03.lead: HC control under Art 235 must respect legal service conditions and appeal rights.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — Art 235 saves appeal rights under law
Officer dealt with per service conditions

POL-743-A04.lead: Art 236(a) lists all three as 'district judge'.

POL-743-A05.lead: Art 236(a) includes all four of these offices.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Chief and additional chief presidency magistrate

POL-743-A06.lead: Both additional and assistant sessions judges are 'district judges' under Art 236(a).
POL-743-A06.also: Art 236(a) also lists the sessions judge itself.

POL-743-A07.lead: The district judge is also sessions judge and has administrative duties too.

POL-743-A08.lead: Subordinate judge = Senior Division; munsiff = Junior Division civil judge.
points: Option 2 reverses the order: the munsiff is the lowest civil court.
Options 3 and 4 mix civil courts with criminal, executive or High Court tiers.

POL-743-A09.lead: Both are true: small causes courts and village panchayat courts exist.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Village panchayat courts in some States

POL-743-A10.lead: Nyaya Panchayat, Gram Kutchery, Adalati Panchayat, Panchayat Adalat are local names.
points: Option 1 lists regular civil and criminal courts.
Option 3 lists administrative tribunals.
Option 4 lists specialised civil courts, not panchayat courts.

POL-743-A11.lead: The 42nd Amendment, 1976 added the All India Judicial Service to Art 312.
points: The 20th Amendment (1966) inserted Art 233A.
The 7th (1956) reorganised States; the 75th (1993) added rent tribunals.
POL-743-A11.also: AIJS posts cannot be below district judge rank (Art 312(3)).

POL-743-A12.lead: Rajya Sabha resolution first, then Parliament creates the service by law.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: RS resolution by two-thirds present and voting

POL-743-A13.lead: Art 312(4): such changes are allowed and not treated as an Art 368 amendment.
points: So Parliament can amend Chapter VI by ordinary law for AIJS.
The Governor has no role, and such changes are not prohibited.
Option 3 swaps the years of the 77th and 116th reports.
Option 4 lists constitutional amendments, not Law Commission reports.

POL-743-A15.lead: Sessions death sentences always need High Court confirmation, appeal or not.
points: BNSS 22(2): a Sessions Judge may pass any lawful sentence, including death.
BNSS 407(1): the death sentence cannot be executed until the High Court confirms it.
The Governor cannot replace this judicial confirmation.

POL-743-A16.lead: A CJM may impose any sentence except death, life, or above seven years.
points: So seven years' imprisonment is within power; eight years is not.
Death and life imprisonment need a Court of Session.

POL-743-A17.lead: First class: 3 years/Rs 50,000; second class: 1 year/Rs 10,000.
points: Option 1 has the original CrPC 1973 fine limits (Rs 5,000 / Rs 1,000).
Seven years is the Chief Judicial Magistrate's limit.
Option 3 reverses the two classes.

POL-743-A18.lead: Community service is allowed, but the convict gets no pay for it.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Community service for both magistrate classes

POL-743-A18.also: Community service is new in BNSS; it was not in CrPC 1973.

POL-743-A19.lead: BNSS 6: Sessions, JM first class, JM second class, Executive Magistrates.
points: BNSS dropped Metropolitan Magistrates as a class.
Small causes, city civil and family courts are civil courts, not BNSS criminal courts.

POL-743-A20.lead: Pending investigations continue under the old CrPC, 1973.
points: BNSS 531(2)(a) saves pending appeals, trials, inquiries and investigations.
There is no free choice of Code and no need for fresh investigation.

POL-743-A21.lead: Rejanish: seven years' combined experience and age 35; selection still required.
POL-743-A21.also: Constitution Bench held in-service judicial officers can compete for direct district-judge recruitment.

POL-743-A22.lead: Para 170 makes the ruling prospective, sparing earlier completed appointments.
points: It does not invalidate past appointments.
Interim-order cases form a stated exception, not a bar on further orders.

POL-743-A23.lead: Art 233(1) covers appointment, posting and promotion of district judges.
points: The Governor must consult the High Court for all three.
The State PSC is not consulted for district judges, and no circular can remove consultation.

POL-743-A24.lead: Art 233A validates only specified past appointments, not future ones.

POL-743-A25.lead: Art 235 names posting, promotion and grant of leave.
POL-743-A25.also: This control covers officers below district judge rank.

POL-743-A26.lead: Art 237: Governor may apply provisions from a date, with exceptions and changes.
points: Application is not automatic or uniform; it depends on the notification.
The Governor, not Parliament, issues it; it creates no All India service.

POL-743-A27.lead: S.25 revision checks legality; s.27 finality is subject to the Act.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: HC revision: was it according to law

POL-743-CH-01.lead: Art 50 directs separation of the judiciary from the executive.

POL-743-CH-02.lead: Art 235 vests control of subordinate courts in the High Court.

POL-743-CH-03.lead: Art 236(a) includes the sessions judge in 'district judge'.
points: The Attorney General, CAG and tribunal heads are not judicial service offices.

POL-743-CH-04.lead: Art 236(b): district judge and civil judicial posts below it.
points: High Court judges are not part of the 'judicial service'.
General civil services and tribunals are outside it.

POL-743-CH-05.lead: Art 237: the Governor extends these provisions to magistrates by notification.
points: Neither the President nor Parliament issues this notification.
The High Court only controls; it does not notify the extension.
It followed Chandra Mohan v State of UP (1966), which struck down irregular appointments.
The 42nd Amendment added AIJS to Art 312.

POL-743-P323-01.lead: The Governor appoints district judges, consulting the High Court.
points: Article 233 gives the power to the Governor of the State, not the President.
The Chief Minister and State PSC have no say in district judge appointments.
Eligibility: an advocate of at least 7 years' standing, recommended by the High Court.

POL-743-P323-02.lead: Article 234 needs consultation with both the State PSC and High Court.
points: Article 234 covers judicial service posts other than district judges, e.g. civil judges.

POL-743-P324-01.lead: Article 312(3): AIJS cannot include any post below district judge.
points: High Court judges are constitutional posts, not part of any civil service.
Civil judges and magistrates rank below district judge, so they are kept out.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) added the All India Judicial Service to Article 312.
POL-743-P324-01.also: An AIJS needs a Rajya Sabha resolution and a law by Parliament; none has been created yet.

POL-743-P324-02.lead: State laws set up subordinate courts, so names and structure vary.
points: Municipal bodies have no power over court structure.
Parliament does not choose courts every year.
The Supreme Court does not prescribe one uniform scheme; each State legislates for its own courts.

POL-743-SJ-PRACTICE-01.lead: Sessions-level trial appeals go to High Court; Magistrate trial appeals go to Sessions Court.
points: Under BNSS Section 415, any trial by a Sessions or Additional Sessions Judge is appealed to the High Court.
A Magistrate's conviction goes to the Court of Session, unless the sentence exceeds seven years.
Option 4 is wrong: confirmation applies to death sentences, not five-year terms.

LX-PQ-075.lead: CAT handles recruitment and all service matters of covered Union employees.
points: Recruitment, promotion and discipline are each only one part of its work.
Article 323A and the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 cover all service conditions.

LX-UPSC-2013-Q07.lead: Both statements describe NALSA's statutory role correctly.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: Free, competent legal aid to weaker sections

points: NALSA was set up under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; it began work in 1995.
LX-UPSC-2013-Q07.also: The Chief Justice of India is NALSA's Patron-in-Chief.

LX-UPSC-2018-Q14.lead: Only statement 2 is correct; CPCB is also a statutory body.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: NGT by Act, CPCB by executive order
False — CPCB set up under Water Act, 1974
NGT gives environmental justice; CPCB fights pollution

points: NGT was set up under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.

LX-UPSC-2019-Q15.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are correct; PNGRB was not the first regulator.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: False — SEBI, TRAI and others came earlier
True — a stated aim of the PNGRB Act
True — Appellate Tribunal for Electricity hears them

points: PNGRB was created under the PNGRB Act, 2006.

POL-744-A01.lead: Tribunals give expert, quasi-judicial decisions within a limited subject area.
points: They do not have unlimited civil and criminal jurisdiction like regular courts.
Their decisions bind parties, so they are not mere advisers.
They are created by law, unlike private arbitration panels chosen by parties.

POL-744-A02.lead: Civilian defence staff are covered; armed forces and SC/Parliament staff are excluded.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: True — civilians in defence services fall under CAT
False — armed forces members are excluded

POL-744-A02.also: Armed forces service disputes go to the Armed Forces Tribunal (2007 Act).

POL-744-A03.lead: Promotion denial is a service dispute; a theft trial is criminal prosecution.
points: Option 1 swaps the two categories.
Being an employee does not make a criminal case a CAT matter.
Both matters are decided by a forum — tribunal or criminal court.

POL-744-A04.lead: An applicant may appear personally or use a lawyer of choice.
points: Section 23 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 allows this.
A presenting officer represents the government, not the applicant.
No rule requires a senior advocate or bars lawyers.

POL-744-A05.lead: SAT on State request and JAT for two or more States are correct.

True/False — why
rows: Centre sets up SAT on State request
JAT for two or more States

POL-744-A06.lead: Taxation, foreign exchange, labour disputes and land reforms are all in Article 323B.
points: Citizenship, passports, divorce and impeachment are not listed in Article 323B.
Public-service recruitment belongs to Article 323A, not 323B.
POL-744-A06.also: Article 323B tribunals can be set up by Parliament or State legislatures, within their legislative powers.

POL-744-A07.lead: All four subjects are listed in Article 323B(2).

POL-744-A08.lead: Article 323B(3)(a) allows a hierarchy of tribunals for non-service subjects.
points: Article 323A has no hierarchy clause; Article 323B does.

POL-744-A09.lead: Legal-services bodies give free legal aid, hold Lok Adalats and spread legal awareness.
points: Awareness camps alone are only part of the work.
They do not collect court fees or prosecute criminal cases.
Lok Adalats mainly handle pending and pre-litigation cases, not decided appeals.

POL-744-A10.lead: Free legal service covers litigation costs like counsel, certified copies and translation.
points: Section 2(1)(c) defines legal service as any service in conducting a case, including advice.
Regulations cover process fees, certified copies, paper-book printing and translation.
Appeals are covered; the right does not end with the trial.

POL-744-A11.lead: Women, children and SC/ST members qualify regardless of income.

head: Stmt

POL-762-CH-08.lead: Courts review policy only for illegality or constitutional violation.
points: Policy-making belongs to the executive; courts do not judge its wisdom.
Dislike, media attention or the lack of a referendum are not grounds for review.

POL-762-P304-01.lead: PIL relaxed locus standi so others can sue for genuine public injury.
points: Evidence is still needed; there is no jury trial in India.
Courts do not take over law-making through PIL.

POL-762-P305-01.lead: A PIL filed for personal publicity, not public interest, should be rejected.
points: Genuine public injury, bona fide representation and an enforceable duty support a PIL.
'Publicity Interest Litigation' is a recognised form of PIL misuse.

POL-8.1.1-Q01.lead: Part XI, Arts 245-255 (11 Articles) cover legislative relations.
points: Arts 256-263 deal with administrative relations.
Part XII (Arts 264-300) deals with finance.
Arts 239-242 deal with Union Territories.
POL-8.1.1-Q01.also: Legislative + administrative = Part XI; financial = Part XII.

POL-8.1.1-Q02.lead: Art 245(1) gives the territorial reach; 245(2) protects extra-territorial laws.
points: Statement 3 is wrong: Art 245(2) says no Parliamentary law is invalid for extra-territorial operation.

POL-8.1.1-Q03.lead: Only Parliament can make laws operating on Indians and property abroad.
points: State laws are confined to the state, subject only to territorial nexus.
The President's regulation power is limited to certain UTs.

POL-8.1.1-Q04.lead: Sufficient nexus between state and object lets a state law reach outside.
points: Pith and substance decides which list a law falls under.
Colourable legislation strikes down disguised encroachment.
Eclipse relates to pre-Constitution laws violating Fundamental Rights.

POL-8.1.1-Q05.lead: Delhi has its own legislature under Art 239AA, not under Art 240.
points: A&N, Lakshadweep, Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu, and Ladakh are covered.
Puducherry is covered only when its Assembly is suspended or dissolved.
POL-8.1.1-Q05.also: Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu became one UT in 2020.

POL-8.1.1-Q06.lead: Fifth Schedule empowers the Governor for Scheduled Areas.
points: The Chief Minister and Home Minister have no such power.
The Tribes Advisory Council only advises the Governor.
For tribal areas: Assam's Governor; President for Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram.

POL-8.1.1-Q07.lead: The 1935 Act had Federal, Provincial and Concurrent lists.
points: Canada gave India the residuary-with-Centre idea, not the three lists.
Australia inspired the Concurrent List concept, but the three-list scheme came from 1935.
The 1919 Act only divided central and provincial subjects.

POL-8.1.1-Q08.lead: After the 101st Amendment: Union 98, State 59, Concurrent 52.
points: The older counts 100/61/52 predate the 2016 GST amendment.
Original 1950 counts were 97/66/47.

POL-8.1.1-Q09.lead: The Union List originally had 97 entries.
points: 66 was the original State List.
47 was the original Concurrent List.
100 counts every added entry but ignores deletions.

POL-8.1.1-Q10.lead: Opium (Entry 59) and Census (Entry 69) are Union subjects.
points: Intoxicating liquors, not opium, are a State subject.
Vital statistics, not census, are in the Concurrent List.

POL-8.1.1-Q11.lead: Atomic energy Union; money-lending and gambling State; bankruptcy Concurrent.
points: Bankruptcy is Concurrent Entry 9.
Money-lending is State Entry 30; betting and gambling State Entry 34.

POL-8.1.1-Q12.lead: Entry 2A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
points: The 7th Amendment deleted Entry 33.
The 46th Amendment added Entry 92B.
The 44th Amendment did not touch this entry.
92A came first in 1956, well before the Emergency-era 42nd Amendment.
92C was inserted in 2003 and deleted in 2016.

POL-8.1.1-Q14.lead: Entry 33 was deleted earlier, by the 7th Amendment, 1956.
points: Entries 92 and 92C were deleted by the 101st Amendment.
Acquisition of property then became Concurrent Entry 42.

POL-8.1.1-Q15.lead: Amended Entry 84 keeps excise on petroleum items and tobacco only.
points: Textiles, cement and phones moved under GST.
Petroleum crude, HSD, petrol, natural gas and ATF also remain under excise.

POL-8.1.1-Q16.lead: 66 originally, 59 now; no entry has ever been added.
points: The 42nd Amendment only removed entries from the State List.
Seven entries were deleted: 11, 19, 20, 29, 36, 52, 55.

POL-8.1.1-Q17.lead: Entry 36 in 1956, Entry 11 in 1976, Entry 52 in 2016.
points: 7th Amendment 1956 removed Entry 36.
42nd Amendment 1976 removed Entry 11.
101st Amendment 2016 removed Entry 52.

POL-8.1.1-Q18.lead: Marriage and divorce is a Concurrent subject (Entry 5).
points: Police, public health and prisons are State subjects.

POL-8.1.1-Q19.lead: Concurrent List began with 47 entries; it now has 52.
points: 52 is the present number.
66 was the original State List.
61 was the State List before 2016.

POL-8.1.1-Q20.lead: Agriculture has always remained a State subject.
points: The five moved were education, forests, weights and measures, wild animals and birds, administration of justice.

POL-8.1.1-Q21.lead: Entry 11A excludes the Supreme Court and High Courts.

head: Statement
Verdict
rows: 1. All courts except SC and HCs

points: Constitution and organisation of High Courts is Union Entry 78.
The Supreme Court is Union Entry 77.
17B covers wild animals and birds.
Education was merged into existing Entry 25, not given a new number.

POL-8.1.1-Q23.lead: 20A was a fresh subject, not a transfer from the State List.
points: The five transferred: education, forests, weights and measures, wildlife, administration of justice.
So A is true and R is false.

POL-8.1.1-Q24.lead: Public order is State List Entry 1.
points: Economic and social planning is Concurrent Entry 20.
Social security is Entry 23; trade unions Entry 22.
Water and gas are State subjects, but electricity is Concurrent.
Atomic energy, not electricity, is in the Union List.

POL-8.1.1-Q26.lead: Parliament may legislate on any matter for areas outside states.
points: No Rajya Sabha resolution or emergency is needed for a UT.
The State List binds only states, not Union Territories.

POL-8.1.1-Q27.lead: Art 246A gives concurrent GST power; inter-state GST is Parliament's alone.
points: Statement 3 is wrong: Parliament has exclusive power over IGST on inter-state supply.
POL-8.1.1-Q27.also: Art 248 was made 'subject to Art 246A' by the same amendment.

POL-8.1.1-Q28.lead: Art 247 allows additional courts for Union laws.
points: Art 245 is territorial extent.
Art 248 is residuary power.
Art 250 is legislation during emergency.

POL-8.1.1-Q29.lead: All three are correct; Art 248(2) covers residuary taxation.
points: Entry 97 of the Union List covers 'any other matter' not in Lists II or III.

POL-8.1.1-Q30.lead: USA states; Canada Centre; 1935 Governor-General; India Parliament.
points: Australia, like the USA, leaves residuary powers with states.
India followed Canada's model.

POL-8.1.1-Q31.lead: Canada vests residuary power in the Centre.
points: USA, Australia and Switzerland leave it with the units.

POL-8.1.1-Q32.lead: The Wild Life Act 1972 was made under Art 252.
points: Wealth tax, gift tax and the Commissions of Inquiry Act rest on residuary power.

POL-8.1.1-Q33.lead: Union List prevails over Concurrent, which prevails over State.
points: Art 246 opens with 'notwithstanding' clauses that set this order.

POL-8.1.1-Q34.lead: Art 254(1) general rule; 254(2) exception, still subject to Parliament.
points: Statement 3 is wrong: the proviso to Art 254(2) lets Parliament add to, amend, vary or repeal it.

POL-8.1.1-Q35.lead: Adulteration is Concurrent; Art 254(1) makes Central law prevail.
points: Only President's assent under Art 254(2) could save the State law.
Only the repugnant part of the State law fails, not both laws.

POL-8.1.1-Q36.lead: R is the very provision that produces A.
points: The exception holds only within that State.
Parliament can later override it by a fresh law.

POL-8.1.1-Q37.lead: Only the Rajya Sabha passes the Art 249 resolution.
points: Statement 2 is wrong: Lok Sabha has no role in the resolution; it only joins in passing the law later.
POL-8.1.1-Q37.also: Rajya Sabha acts here as the Council of States guarding federal balance.

POL-8.1.1-Q38.lead: Art 249 needs a Rajya Sabha resolution by 2/3 present and voting.
points: Lok Sabha has no role in the resolution.
State ratification applies to some amendments, not Art 249.

POL-8.1.1-Q39.lead: Resolution lasts one year; law lapses six months after that.
points: 1 March 2026 is when the resolution ends, not the law.
The law is temporary; only Art 252 laws are permanent in effect.

POL-8.1.1-Q40.lead: State power is not taken away; Parliament's law merely prevails on conflict.
points: Statement 2 is wrong: the State keeps concurrent power over the matter.

POL-8.1.1-Q41.lead: Art 250(2): such laws lapse six months after emergency.
points: Repeal by the State legislature is the rule for laws made during President's Rule.
One year is the life of an Art 249 resolution.

POL-8.1.1-Q42.lead: Art 251 is the rule that makes the State law inoperative.
points: The State law is only suspended, not permanently void.

POL-8.1.1-Q43.lead: Art 252 law binds only consenting States; others may adopt it later.
points: Statement 2 is wrong: other States adopt it only by their own resolution.

POL-8.1.1-Q44.lead: Under Art 252(2), only Parliament can amend or repeal it.
points: The requesting States surrender their power over that matter.
No time limit or partner consent restores it.

POL-8.1.1-Q45.lead: The Anti-Hijacking Act 1982 implemented international conventions under Art 253.
points: The other three are Art 252 laws, as are Wild Life Act 1972 and Urban Land Ceiling Act 1976.

POL-8.1.1-Q46.lead: Urban Land Art 252; Geneva Art 253; Gift Tax residuary.
points: Urban Land Ceiling came after State resolutions.
Geneva Conventions Act gives effect to treaties.

POL-8.1.1-Q47.lead: Art 253 overrides the list division for treaty implementation.
points: No State consent or resolution is required under Art 253.
Examples: UN (Privileges and Immunities) Act 1947, TRIPS-related laws.

POL-8.1.1-Q48.lead: President's Rule laws survive; emergency laws lapse after six months.
points: Statement 2 is wrong: Art 250(2) ends them six months after the emergency.

POL-8.1.1-Q49.lead: Art 255 treats sanction requirements as procedural; later assent cures the defect.
points: No parliamentary ratification or time limit applies.

POL-8.1.1-Q50.lead: 201 veto, 304 trade sanction, 360 money bills, 213 ordinance.
points: Art 200 lets the Governor reserve; Art 201 is the President's decision.
Art 304(b) needs sanction before introduction.

POL-8.1.1-Q51.lead: The President can withhold assent and the State cannot override it.
points: Even if the State re-passes the bill, the President need not assent.

POL-8.1.1-Q52.lead: The Sarkaria Commission defended federal supremacy as indispensable.
points: Rajamannar (Tamil Nadu, 1969) sought more State autonomy.
Punchhi (2007) came later and dealt broadly with Centre-State relations.

POL-8.1.1-Q53.lead: The true character decides the list; incidental encroachment is ignored.
points: Colourable legislation strikes down disguised encroachment.
Repugnancy deals with conflicting laws on the same Concurrent subject.
POL-8.1.1-Q53.also: Leading case: Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee v Bank of Commerce, Khulna (1947).

POL-8.1.1-Q54.lead: G. Chawla (1959) applied pith and substance to a State law on loudspeakers.
points: Gajapati Narayan Deo is the colourable legislation case.
Kesavananda Bharati and Minerva Mills concern the basic structure doctrine.

POL-8.1.1-Q55.lead: R states the doctrine whose maxim is A.
points: Leading case: K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v State of Orissa (1953).

POL-8.1.1-Q56.lead: Lists are federal provisions under the proviso to Art 368(2).
points: Unanimous State ratification is never required.
Special majority alone suffices for non-federal provisions.

POL-8.1.1-Q57.lead: Art 246 links the three lists to the two legislatures.
points: Art 245 is about territorial extent.
Art 248 is residuary power; Art 254 is repugnancy.

POL-8.1.2-Q01.lead: Part XI, Chapter II (Arts 256-263) covers administrative relations.
points: Arts 245-255 are legislative relations (Part XI, Ch. I).
Arts 264-300 are finance, property and contracts (Part XII).
Arts 301-307 cover trade and commerce (Part XIII).
POL-8.1.2-Q01.also: Arts 256-263 make 8 Articles, one (259) now repealed.

POL-8.1.2-Q02.lead: Concurrent List executive power normally stays with states.
points: Statement 1 reflects Art.73.
Statement 2 is wrong: states hold it unless the Constitution or a Parliament law gives it to the Centre.

POL-8.1.2-Q03.lead: Concurrent executive power vests in states unless expressly given to Centre.
points: The Centre gets it only if the Constitution or the law says so (e.g. Essential Commodities Act functions).
The President cannot take it by an order alone.
The ISC is only advisory.

POL-8.1.2-Q04.lead: Art.256 sets the obligation of states and Union directions.
points: Art.254 deals with repugnancy between Central and state laws.
Art.258 is delegation of Union functions to states.
Art.262 is inter-state river water disputes.

POL-8.1.2-Q05.lead: Art.257(1) bars states from impeding Union executive power.
points: Art.256 is about complying with Parliament's laws.
Art.258A lets the Governor entrust state functions to Centre.
Art.261 is full faith and credit.
Option 2 swaps the two clauses of Art.257.
Options 3 and 4 swap Art.350A and Art.339(2).

POL-8.1.2-Q07.lead: Art.257(4): the Centre pays the state's extra costs.
points: Statement 1 is Art.257(3).
Statement 2 is wrong: the amount is agreed or fixed by an arbitrator appointed by the CJI and paid by the Centre.

POL-8.1.2-Q08.lead: Art.257(4) provides an arbitrator appointed by the CJI.
points: Finance Commission recommends tax devolution, not such costs.
CAG audits accounts only.
ISC is advisory and has no such role.

POL-8.1.2-Q09.lead: Salary cuts can be directed only in a Financial Emergency (Art.360).
points: Railways: Art.257(3).
Mother tongue: Art.350A.
ST welfare: Art.339(2).

POL-8.1.2-Q10.lead: Art.365 links non-compliance to Art.356 President's Rule.
points: A is true: non-compliance is a ground for Art.356.
R is true and explains A: Art.365 creates the deeming provision.

POL-8.1.2-Q11.lead: Art.365 deals with effect of failure to comply with Union directions.
points: Art.355 is the Union's duty to protect states.
Art.360 is Financial Emergency.
Art.263 is the Inter-State Council.

POL-8.1.2-Q12.lead: Art.258(1) needs the consent of the state government.
points: Parliament acts separately under Art.258(2) through a law.
Courts and the ISC have no role in delegation.
POL-8.1.2-Q12.also: Delegation may be conditional or unconditional.

POL-8.1.2-Q13.lead: Delegation without consent needs a Parliament law (Art.258(2)).
points: Statement 1 is Art.258(2).
Statement 2 is wrong: the President needs the state's consent under Art.258(1).
1st Amendment added the Ninth Schedule.
42nd and 44th Amendments did not touch Art.258A.

POL-8.1.2-Q15.lead: Art.258: President to state; Art.258A: Governor to Centre.
points: Art.258 is the original one-way route (1950).
Art.258A, added in 1956, created the reverse route.
No Article provides state-to-state delegation.

POL-8.1.2-Q16.lead: Executive delegation is allowed; legislative delegation is not.
points: A is true under Arts 258 and 258A.
R is false: legislative distribution is rigid and cannot be delegated.

POL-8.1.2-Q17.lead: 7th Amendment abolished Part A/B/C states and omitted Art.259.
points: 24th Amendment concerned Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights.
42nd Amendment is the 'mini-Constitution', not this repeal.
5th Amendment dealt with state views on reorganisation bills.

POL-8.1.2-Q18.lead: Art.260 covers Union jurisdiction over territories outside India.
points: Art.253 lets Parliament legislate to implement treaties.
Art.261 is full faith and credit.
Art.73 is the extent of Union executive power.

POL-8.1.2-Q19.lead: Art.261 is the full faith and credit clause.
points: Art.256: compliance with Parliament's laws.
Art.262: river water disputes.
Art.263: Inter-State Council.

POL-8.1.2-Q20.lead: Art.261(3): final judgments are executable anywhere in India.
points: Art.262 concerns river water disputes.
Art.258A is delegation from state to Centre.
Art.307 concerns an authority for inter-state trade.

POL-8.1.2-Q21.lead: Art.262(1) and 262(2) give both powers to Parliament.
points: Clause (1): adjudication of disputes.
Clause (2): exclusion of jurisdiction of the SC or any other court.

POL-8.1.2-Q22.lead: ISRWD Act, 1956 provides for ad hoc tribunals.
points: River Boards Act, 1956 is for river boards, not tribunals.
The other two Acts do not exist; National Water Policy is a policy.
POL-8.1.2-Q22.also: Krishna and Godavari tribunals were set up under this Act.

POL-8.1.2-Q23.lead: Both are features of the ISRWD Act after 2002.
points: Statement 1: Section 11 bars court jurisdiction.
Statement 2: Section 6(2), added in 2002, gives the award decree-like force.
POL-8.1.2-Q23.also: SC still hears appeals against awards under Art.136 (Cauvery, 2018).

POL-8.1.2-Q24.lead: Art.263 lets the President set up the Council by order.
points: The PM chairs it but does not create it.
No Parliamentary law is needed.
The Home Minister is only a member.

POL-8.1.2-Q25.lead: ISC is advisory; river disputes go to Art.262 tribunals.
points: Options 1-3 are the three duties listed in Art.263(a)-(c).
Binding water awards come from tribunals under the ISRWD Act.

POL-8.1.2-Q26.lead: Members also include six Union ministers and Governors under President's Rule.
points: Statement 1: Presidential order of 1990.
Statement 2: PM is ex-officio chairman.
Statement 3 is wrong: Union Cabinet ministers and CMs of UTs with legislatures are also members.

POL-8.1.2-Q27.lead: The CJI has no place in an executive coordination body.
points: UT CMs with legislatures are members.
Governors of states under President's Rule are members.
Six Cabinet ministers, including the Home Minister, are members.
POL-8.1.2-Q27.also: Union Home Minister is a member; Cabinet ministers can be permanent invitees too.

POL-8.1.2-Q28.lead: No Art.307 authority has ever been appointed.
points: Statement 1 is correct (Part XIII).
Statement 2 is wrong: Parliament has not appointed any such authority so far.

POL-8.1.2-Q29.lead: ISC 263, water 262, faith and credit 261, trade 307.
points: Option 2 swaps Arts 262 and 263.
Option 3 swaps Arts 261 and 307.
Option 4 swaps Arts 261 and 263.

POL-8.1.2-Q30.lead: Indian Foreign Service is a Central Service, not an AIS.
points: IAS, IPS and IFoS are the three All-India Services.
IFS officers serve only under the Centre.

POL-8.1.2-Q31.lead: Ultimate control is with the Centre; immediate control with the state.
points: Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2 reverses the position: states have only immediate control.
ICS became IAS in 1947.
The 7th Amendment came in 1956.
IFoS was created in 1966; ISC in 1990.

POL-8.1.2-Q33.lead: Art.312 needs two-thirds of RS members present and voting.
points: Simple majority is not enough.
The other two thresholds are not used in Art.312.
POL-8.1.2-Q33.also: Same majority is used under Art.249 for State List laws in national interest.

POL-8.1.2-Q34.lead: Central control over top state officers draws the federal criticism.
points: A is true: critics make this point.
R is true and is the very reason for the criticism.
POL-8.1.2-Q34.also: Justification: high standards, uniformity, coordination; Ambedkar backed AIS for strategic posts.

POL-8.1.2-Q35.lead: Art.317: SPSC members are removable only by the President.
points: The Governor can only suspend pending an SC inquiry on misbehaviour.
CM and state legislature have no removal power.
POL-8.1.2-Q35.also: Purpose: insulate SPSC from state-level political pressure.

points: Statement 1: Art.315(2), by a Parliament law on state resolutions.
Statement 2: Art.315(4).
POL-8.1.2-Q36.also: UPSC also assists states in joint recruitment for specially qualified posts.

POL-8.1.2-Q37.lead: Art.217: consultation with the CJI and the Governor.
points: For puisne judges the HC Chief Justice is also consulted.
The CM, Law Ministers and SPSC are not constitutional consultees.
POL-8.1.2-Q37.also: President can also transfer (Art.222) and remove HC judges.

POL-8.1.2-Q38.lead: Art.231 lets Parliament establish a common High Court.
points: The SC cannot create courts.
State legislatures cannot set up a shared HC.
ISC is only advisory.
POL-8.1.2-Q38.also: Examples: Bombay HC (Maharashtra, Goa); Punjab & Haryana HC; Gauhati HC.

POL-8.1.2-Q39.lead: AP and Telangana have separate High Courts since 1 January 2019.
points: Bombay HC serves Maharashtra and Goa.
Punjab and Haryana HC serves both states and Chandigarh.
Gauhati HC serves Assam and Nagaland (also Mizoram, Arunachal).

POL-8.1.2-Q40.lead: Art.353 any matter; Art.356 takeover; Art.360 financial directions.
points: Option 2 swaps National Emergency and President's Rule.
Options 3 and 4 misplace the financial directions.

POL-8.1.2-Q41.lead: Art.353(a) extends Union executive power to directions on any matter.
points: Art.352 is the proclamation itself.
Art.354 concerns distribution of revenues.
Art.358 suspends Art.19.

POL-8.1.2-Q42.lead: Salary-cut directions are a Financial Emergency power.
points: Art.356 is about takeover of state government, not salary cuts.
Art.256 is about compliance with Parliament's laws.
Art.352 allows directions on any matter but salary reduction is the Art.360 power.
POL-8.1.2-Q42.also: Art.360(4)(b) separately lets the President direct reduction of salaries of SC and HC judges. Financial Emergency has never been declared in India.

POL-8.1.2-Q43.lead: Art.355 imposes this duty on the Union.
points: Art.352 is National Emergency proclamation.
Art.356 is President's Rule, which Art.355 justifies.
Art.365 is non-compliance with directions.
POL-8.1.2-Q43.also: Art.355 also requires that every state be governed per the Constitution.

POL-8.1.2-Q44.lead: Art.355 duty is the constitutional basis for Art.356.
points: A is true under Art.356.
R is true and explains A: Art.356 is the means to discharge the Art.355 duty.

POL-8.1.2-Q45.lead: SEC is removable only like a High Court judge (Art.243K).
points: Statement 1: Art.156; the Governor also reports to the Centre.
Statement 2 is wrong: Governor appoints the SEC but cannot remove at pleasure.

POL-8.1.2-Q46.lead: Finance Commission is a constitutional body (Art.280).
points: NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission in 2015.
NIC and NEC are non-constitutional bodies.
Zonal Councils and UGC are also in this list.
POL-8.1.2-Q46.also: Zonal Councils and NEC are statutory, not constitutional.

POL-8.1.2-Q47.lead: Governors-President, CMs-PM, Chief Secretaries-Cabinet Secretary, CJs-CJI.
points: Option 2 swaps President and PM.
Option 3 swaps Cabinet Secretary and CJI.
Option 4 swaps PM and Cabinet Secretary.

POL-8.1.2-Q48.lead: Zonal Councils are statutory (States Reorganisation Act, 1956).
points: Statement 1 is wrong: only the ISC was set up under Art.263.
Statement 2 is correct: NITI Aayog came on 1 January 2015.

POL-8.2.1-Q01.lead: Legislative and administrative are in Part XI; financial in Part XII.
points: Arts 245-255 come first, followed by 256-263 in the same Part.
Finance starts at Art 264 in Part XII.
Counting 245 through 255 gives 11.
8 is the count for administrative relations (256-263).

POL-8.2.1-Q03.lead: India has one integrated judiciary enforcing both Union and state laws.
points: Legislative, executive and financial powers are divided under Parts XI and XII.
Unlike the USA, there are no separate federal and state courts.

POL-8.2.1-Q04.lead: Art 245(2) protects extra-territorial Union laws; states are confined to their territory.

head: Statement
Verdict
rows: 1. Union law not invalid for extra-territoriality
2. State law for any part of India

points: Statement 2 is wrong: Art 245(1) limits a state to the whole or part of that state.
Only Parliament has extra-territorial legislative power.

POL-8.2.1-Q05.lead: Operation beyond India's borders is saved by Art 245(2).
points: Art 246(3) concerns the State List, not territory.
Art 248 is about subject, not territorial reach.
Art 252 needs state resolutions and has nothing to do with acts abroad.

POL-8.2.1-Q06.lead: A real nexus lets a state law reach objects outside its borders.
points: Pith and substance decides which list a law falls in.
Colourable legislation is disguised transgression.
Eclipse concerns pre-Constitution laws and Fundamental Rights.

POL-8.2.1-Q07.lead: Chandigarh is not listed in Art 240.
points: The other three are named in Art 240(1).
Puducherry is covered only when its legislature is suspended or dissolved.
POL-8.2.1-Q07.also: A regulation under Art 240 has the same force as an Act of Parliament and can amend one.

POL-8.2.1-Q08.lead: In Assam it is the Governor; in the other three NE states, the President.
points: Statement 3 is wrong: the Governor of Assam holds this Sixth Schedule power.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct exceptions to Parliament's territorial reach.

POL-8.2.1-Q09.lead: The 1935 Act created Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists.
points: Canada has two lists only.
The USA lists only federal powers.
The 1919 Act had central and provincial subjects, not three lists.

POL-8.2.1-Q10.lead: Clause order is Union, Concurrent, then State.
points: Concurrent is in clause (2), before State in clause (3).
Clause (4) deals with Union Territories.

POL-8.2.1-Q11.lead: Originally 97 Union, 66 State and 47 Concurrent entries.
points: Figures like 52 for the Concurrent List are present-day counts after 1976.
State List count fell after transfers and omissions.

POL-8.2.1-Q12.lead: The 42nd Amendment inserted five new Concurrent entries (11A, 17A, 17B, 20A, 33A), taking 47 to 52.

head: Statement
Verdict
rows: R: five new entries inserted in 1976

points: 47 + 5 new entries = 52, so R explains A.
Education was added by widening Entry 25, so it added no new entry; population control (20A) was a new subject, not a transfer.

POL-8.2.1-Q13.lead: Census is Union, trade unions Concurrent, prisons and gambling State.
points: Prisons is State List Entry 4.
Trade unions is Concurrent Entry 22.
Betting and gambling is State Entry 34.

POL-8.2.1-Q14.lead: Public health and sanitation is a State List subject.
points: Atomic energy, banking and railways need national uniformity and are Union subjects.

POL-8.2.1-Q15.lead: Marriage and divorce is a Concurrent List subject.
points: Police, agriculture and money-lending are matters of local importance in the State List.

POL-8.2.1-Q16.lead: All three are Concurrent List entries.
points: Population control (20A) came in 1976; electricity and newspapers were there from 1950.
Residuary subjects are those in no list.

Verdict

Verdict

Verdict

Repugnancy works through Art 254; residuary through Art 248.

ARC reported on administration generally.

Art 249 works even without an Emergency.

Legislature, Parliament or High Court consent is not required.

POL-8.2.2-Q13.lead: Art 261(1) gives the rule; 261(2) leaves proof to Parliament.
points: Public acts include legislative and executive acts.
Public records are official registers kept by public servants.

Civil decrees need no fresh suit in another state.
