POL-8.3.4-Q25.lead: Dr Y.V. Reddy, former RBI Governor, headed the 14th FC.
points: Kelkar 13th; Rangarajan 12th; N.K. Singh 15th.
2010-15 was the 13th FC period; 2020-26 the 15th FC.

POL-8.3.4-Q27.lead: 32% to 42%: the biggest jump in devolution.
points: 15th FC later set it at 41%.
Demographic change (2011) 10%, forest cover 7.5%.
15th FC changed forest cover to 'forest and ecology' at 10%.

POL-8.3.4-Q30.lead: President constituted the 15th FC under N.K. Singh on 27 Nov 2017.
points: 2 Jan 2013: 14th FC.
5 Dec 2019: 15th FC first report.
31 Dec 2023: 16th FC.

POL-8.3.4-Q31.lead: Two reports; award period ran to 2025-26.
points: First report (5 Dec 2019) for 2020-21; second (9 Nov 2020) for 2021-26.
The 1% cut reflected J&K becoming a Union territory.
32% was the 13th FC share.

POL-8.3.4-Q33.lead: ToR mandated 2011 population, favouring populous states.
points: Income distance stayed (45%).
Contribution to GDP was added by the 16th FC.
Vertical share was 41%.
Forest and ecology 10%; area and population 15% each; income distance 45%.
Earlier FCs used 1971 population; the 14th mixed 1971 and 2011.
29 Nov 2023: Cabinet approved ToR.
1 Feb 2026: report tabled in Parliament.
Panagariya was NITI Aayog's first Vice-Chairman (2015-17).

POL-8.3.4-Q38.lead: Shaktikanta Das was a 15th FC member, not 16th.
points: T. Rabi Sankar is the fourth 16th FC member.
Manoj Panda replaced Ajay Narayan Jha.

POL-8.3.4-Q39.lead: ToR included disaster management financing review.
points: GST compensation is a GST Council matter.
Small savings rates are set by the Finance Ministry.
31 Oct 2025 was only the deadline, not the submission date.

POL-8.3.4-Q41.lead: 16th FC retained 41%, same as the 15th FC.
points: 42% was the 14th FC figure.

POL-8.3.4-Q42.lead: Contribution to GDP (10%) is new; tax effort was dropped.
points: Demographic performance came from the 15th FC.
Forest cover has been used since the 14th FC.
Income distance fell from 45% (15th) to 42.5%.
Rs 4.35 lakh crore is for rural local bodies only.
Rs 1.56 lakh crore is for disaster management only.
Chavan headed the 8th FC (1982), Khusro the 11th (1998).
K. Brahmananda Reddy was a former Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister.

POL-8.3.4-Q47.lead: Rangarajan headed the 12th; Vijay Kelkar the 13th.
points: Other pairs are correct.
Santhanam 2nd, Chanda 3rd, Rajamannar 4th.

POL-8.3.4-Q49.lead: 243Y is in Part IXA, not Part IX.
points: Both came through the 73rd and 74th CAA, 1992.

POL-8.3.4-Q50.lead: Governor constitutes the SFC every five years.
points: The President constitutes the Union FC.
The legislature only fixes composition by law.

POL-8.3.4-Q51.lead: Art 243-I(2) leaves composition to state law.
points: The 1+4 size is the Union FC rule, not a constitutional SFC rule.

POL-8.3.4-Q52.lead: Sharing Union taxes among states is the Union FC's job.
points: Options 1, 2 and 4 are SFC functions under Arts 243-I and 243Y.

POL-8.3.4-Q53.lead: Governor causes it to be laid, like the President for the Union FC.
points: Art 243-I(4) names the Governor.

POL-8.3.4-Q54.lead: AP's first SFC came in 1994, after the 73rd CAA.
points: 1992 was the year the 73rd/74th Amendments were passed.

POL-8.3.4-Q55.lead: Chairman needs only experience in public affairs.
points: No degree or MP status is required by the 1951 Act.

POL-8.3.5-Q01.lead: The 122nd Bill became the 101st Amendment Act after enactment.
points: Bill numbers differ from Act numbers; Acts are numbered only on enactment.
The 115th Bill (2011) was the earlier GST Bill that lapsed.
The 124th Bill became the 103rd Act (EWS quota).
POL-8.3.5-Q01.also: GST came into force on 1 July 2017.

POL-8.3.5-Q02.lead: Assam ratified first (Aug 2016); Art 279A came by the 101st CAA.
points: Ratification by half the States was needed as GST affects federal provisions (Art 368(2) proviso).
Bihar was the second State to ratify.

POL-8.3.5-Q03.lead: Art 279A(1) fixes a 60-day window for the President's order.
points: The order was issued on 15 September 2016, within the window.
30 days, 90 days and 6 months are not mentioned in Art 279A.

POL-8.3.5-Q04.lead: Act (8 Sep 2016) → order (15 Sep) → meeting (22-23 Sep) → GST (1 Jul 2017).
points: The Council must exist before it can meet; GST rollout came almost a year later.
The first meeting was chaired by Arun Jaitley in New Delhi.

POL-8.3.5-Q05.lead: Finance Minister Arun Jaitley chaired it as Council Chairperson.
points: The Chairperson is always the Union Finance Minister, not the PM or President.
Nirmala Sitharaman became FM only in 2019.

POL-8.3.5-Q06.lead: FM chairs; State members pick the Vice-Chair; MoS is the second Union member.
points: The Union MoS can never be Vice-Chairperson; that post goes to a State member.
Each State sends one minister.

POL-8.3.5-Q07.lead: Only State members choose the Vice-Chair, for a period they decide.
points: Art 279A(3) gives both the choice and the period to the State members.
The Constitution fixes no tenure for the Vice-Chairperson.

POL-8.3.5-Q08.lead: CBIC handles indirect taxes, so its Chair is a non-voting invitee.
points: CBDT deals with direct taxes like income tax.
CAG and RBI Governor have no role in Council meetings.
This invitee arrangement is a Union Cabinet decision, not in Art 279A.

POL-8.3.5-Q09.lead: A non-member invitee has no vote, so R explains A.
points: Only members listed in Art 279A(2) vote.
Being outside Art 279A, the invitee also does not count for quorum.

POL-8.3.5-Q10.lead: The Revenue Secretary (Department of Revenue) is ex-officio Secretary.
points: The Secretariat is located at New Delhi.
Cabinet Secretary and CEA have no formal Council post.

POL-8.3.5-Q11.lead: Quorum is 1/2; 3/4 is of members present and voting.
points: Art 279A(7) fixes quorum at one-half.
Art 279A(9) counts weighted votes of members present and voting, not total strength.
POL-8.3.5-Q11.also: Do not mix the 1/2 quorum with the 3/4 decision rule.

POL-8.3.5-Q12.lead: Centre 1/3; all States together 2/3 of total votes cast.
points: Two-thirds is the combined weightage of the States.
One-half is the quorum, not a vote weight.
Half of the States' share gives only 66.67% total, short of 75%.
3/4 and 2/3 are the overall threshold and the States' weight, not the needed share.

POL-8.3.5-Q14.lead: 66.67% is below 75%, so R explains A.
points: This gives the Centre a de facto veto.
Likewise the Centre's 33.33% alone cannot pass anything; a large State bloc can block it.

POL-8.3.5-Q15.lead: Only technical defects are saved; lacking the 3/4 majority is not.
points: Vacancy, appointment defect and harmless procedural irregularity are the three saved grounds.
A decision without the Art 279A(9) majority is not a valid decision at all.

POL-8.3.5-Q16.lead: The Council fixes its own procedure under Art 279A(8).
points: Neither Parliament nor the President fixes the Council's procedure.
The vision speaks of the highest standards of co-operative federalism.

POL-8.3.5-Q17.lead: It is the first constitutional federal body taking major GST decisions.
points: It is constitutional (Art 279A), not statutory.
The Inter-State Council (Art 263) is a different, older body.
GSTAT, not the Council, is the tax tribunal.
POL-8.3.5-Q17.also: Its vision: highest standards of co-operative federalism.

POL-8.3.5-Q18.lead: Both are listed recommendation matters under Art 279A(4).
points: The Council also recommends the turnover threshold below which supplies may be exempted.
Its output is recommendation, not law.

POL-8.3.5-Q19.lead: Petroleum date is a separate clause (5); others are in clause (4).
points: Clause (4)(e) covers rates with floor rates and bands.
Clause (4)(d) covers the exemption threshold.

POL-8.3.5-Q20.lead: The threshold limit is a GST Council recommendation under Art 279A(4)(d).
points: The Finance Commission recommends division of taxes under Art 280.
CBIC administers but does not recommend thresholds.
NITI Aayog has no constitutional role in GST.

POL-8.3.5-Q21.lead: GST 2.0 used the Art 279A(4)(e) rate power.
points: GST 2.0 moved most items to 5% and 18% slabs from 22 Sep 2025.
Individual life and health insurance premiums were exempted.
The 12% and 28% slabs were removed for most items.
A separate 40% rate applies to sin/luxury goods.

POL-8.3.5-Q23.lead: The list is the 8 NE States plus J&K, HP and Uttarakhand.
points: Sikkim, HP and Uttarakhand are hill States on the list.
Andhra Pradesh's special category demand never placed it in Art 279A(4)(g).
POL-8.3.5-Q23.also: J&K in the list now refers to the UT after the 2019 Reorganisation Act.

POL-8.3.5-Q24.lead: The five are crude, HSD, petrol, natural gas and ATF.
points: LPG is already within GST.
ATF, natural gas and HSD remain outside GST until the Council recommends a date.

POL-8.3.5-Q25.lead: The Council itself sets up the mechanism under Art 279A(11).
points: Covered: Centre vs State(s); Centre and State(s) vs other State(s); two or more States.
No reference to Parliament, PAC or the Supreme Court is prescribed.

POL-8.3.5-Q26.lead: Centre plus State(s) vs other State(s) is an expressly covered configuration.
points: Art 279A(11) is not limited to Centre vs State.
The Finance Commission and Parliament have no role in such disputes.

POL-8.3.5-Q27.lead: Five years from 1 July 2017 ended on 30 June 2022.
points: Parliament, not the Council, determines compensation by law.
The cess was later continued only to repay loans taken for the Covid-era shortfall.

POL-8.3.5-Q28.lead: Art 246A is concurrent; IGST under Art 269A is Union-levied.
points: Art 246A(2) gives Parliament exclusive power over inter-State supply.
IGST is apportioned between Union and States on Council recommendation.

POL-8.3.5-Q29.lead: The Court held recommendations persuasive, not binding.
points: Parliament and States can legislate simultaneously on GST under Art 246A.
The Court described Indian federalism as a dialogue, both co-operative and uncooperative.
POL-8.3.5-Q29.also: Strengthens the fiscal federalism reading of Art 279A.

POL-8.3.5-Q30.lead: Constitutional status does not make its recommendations binding.
points: Art 279A uses the word 'recommendations'.
The SC in 2022 gave them persuasive value only.

POL-8.3.5-Q31.lead: GST is an indirect tax collected where goods/services are consumed.
points: GST is indirect, not direct.
Being destination-based, revenue goes to the consuming State.
POL-8.3.5-Q31.also: This is why the Centre and States must co-administer it.

POL-8.3.5-Q32.lead: Quorum is one-half of 33, i.e. 16.5, so 17 members.
points: 11 is one-third; 22 is two-thirds; 25 is about three-fourths.
33 = 2 Union members + 31 from States and UTs with legislature.

POL-8.3.5-Q33.lead: Only UTs with a legislature count as 'State' for GST.
points: Delhi, Puducherry and J&K have legislatures, so they are members.
Ladakh is a UT without a legislature.

POL-8.3.5-Q34.lead: The President constitutes the Council; the FM chairs it; Secretariat is in Delhi.
points: The order came on 15 September 2016.
Mumbai hosts RBI, not the GST Council Secretariat.
States (66.67%) also cannot reach 75% without the Centre.
This mutual check reflects fiscal federalism.

POL-8.3.5-Q36.lead: Both are features of the 101st CAA, 2016.
points: The Amendment also inserted Arts 269A and 279A.
States gave up VAT/sales tax powers in return for 5-year compensation.

POL-8.3.6-Q01.lead: NCSC is created directly by Article 338 of the Constitution.
points: NCW was set up in 1992 under the NCW Act, 1990.
NHRC (1993) rests on the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
NCM (1993) rests on the NCM Act, 1992.
NCW Act was passed in 1990 but the body began in 1992.
NCM Act 1992 led to the commission in 1993.
Separate NCSC arose after the 89th CAA came into force in 2004.

POL-8.3.6-Q03.lead: Art 338 creates NCSC, so only an amendment can remove it.

head: Item
Verdict
rows: A: cannot be abolished by ordinary law

points: Ordinary law can change only statutory bodies like NCW or NHRC.
A constitutional body needs a constitutional amendment (Art 368) to be abolished.

POL-8.3.6-Q04.lead: Original Art 338 created one Special Officer for SCs and STs.
points: Multi-member constitutional body came only with the 65th CAA, 1990.
Separate SC-only commission came after the 89th CAA, 2003.
No statutory board was provided.
POL-8.3.6-Q04.also: This officer was designated Commissioner for SCs and STs.

POL-8.3.6-Q05.lead: The officer was the Commissioner and reported to the President.

head: Statement
Verdict
rows: 1. Designated Commissioner for SCs and STs

points: Statement 1 is correct: formal designation was Commissioner for SCs and STs.
Statement 2 is wrong: reports went to the President, not Parliament directly.
The 1931 Census first classified 'depressed classes'.
The GoI Act 1935 first used 'Scheduled Castes'.
65th CAA 1990 gave constitutional status; 89th CAA 2003 split it.

POL-8.3.6-Q07.lead: 1978 body was Resolution-based; the Commissioner's office continued.
points: Statement 1 is correct: it was a non-statutory, multi-member body.
Statement 2 is wrong: both ran in parallel till the 65th CAA replaced them.

POL-8.3.6-Q08.lead: Bhola Paswan Shastri headed the 1978 commission.
points: B.P. Mandal headed the Second Backward Classes Commission (1979).
Kunwar Singh was the first NCST Chairperson (2004).
Jagjivan Ram was a Union Minister, not its head.

POL-8.3.6-Q09.lead: The 1987 Resolution kept it non-statutory, as an advisory body.
points: Constitutional status came only with the 65th CAA, 1990.
No Act of Parliament ever backed it.
It was not a tribunal.

POL-8.3.6-Q10.lead: Enacted in 1990, the 65th CAA took effect on 12 March 1992.
points: 19 Feb 2004 is when the 89th CAA came into force.
The other two dates are not linked to this amendment.

POL-8.3.6-Q11.lead: 65th CAA merged both old bodies into one combined commission.
points: Statements 1 and 2 are correct: both earlier arrangements were replaced at once.
Statement 3 is wrong: the split came with the 89th CAA, 2003.
Art 338B is for NCBC (102nd CAA, 2018).
Art 339 deals with Union control over administration of Scheduled Areas and ST welfare.
Art 340 provides for a Backward Classes Commission.
Statement 1 is correct: 89th CAA, 2003.
Statement 2 is correct: the Act came into force on 19 Feb 2004, creating separate NCSC.
Special Officer: 1950.
Resolution commission: 1978 (renamed 1987).
Constitutional commission: 65th CAA 1990; split: 89th CAA 2003.
338A came by the 89th CAA, 2003.
338B came by the 102nd CAA, 2018.

POL-8.3.6-Q16.lead: 102nd CAA 2018 gave NCBC constitutional status under Art 338B.
points: 89th CAA inserted Art 338A.
101st CAA introduced GST.
103rd CAA gave 10% EWS reservation.
3 counts only the other Members.
4 leaves out one office-bearer.
7 is not the composition of any of these commissions.

POL-8.3.6-Q18.lead: Appointment by warrant; service terms decided by the President.
points: Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 2 is wrong: the President determines conditions of service and tenure (NCSC Rules, 2004).

POL-8.3.6-Q19.lead: Tenure is 3 years; maximum two terms.
points: No third term is allowed in any post.
Parliament has no role in reappointment.
Minister of State rank goes to the Vice-Chairperson.
Members get the rank of Secretary to the Government of India (not Deputy Minister).
SC Judge status is not given.

POL-8.3.6-Q21.lead: Cabinet Minister, Minister of State and Secretary to GoI ranks in that order.
points: Ranks drop with each level of office.
Resignations of all of them go to the President.

POL-8.3.6-Q22.lead: The appointing authority, the President, receives the resignation.
points: PM and Ministers do not appoint members.
The Speaker has no role in NCSC appointment.

POL-8.3.6-Q23.lead: All three are listed functions under Art 338(5).
points: 1: safeguard monitoring is its core watchdog role.
2: grievance redressal for deprivation of rights.
3: planning advice and evaluation of progress under Union/states.

POL-8.3.6-Q24.lead: SC lists are notified by the President under Art 341.
points: Recommendation-making is a listed function.
Art 338(5)(f) allows other functions the President specifies.
Evaluation of safeguards is part of its first function.
POL-8.3.6-Q24.also: Parliament alone can alter the SC list by law (Art 341(2)).

POL-8.3.6-Q25.lead: Both describe the reporting chain under Art 338(5)-(6).
points: Statement 1: annual plus as-and-when reports.
Statement 2: memorandum must give action taken and reasons for non-acceptance.

POL-8.3.6-Q26.lead: Route: Commission to President to Governor to state legislature.
points: The Commission reports only to the President.
Parliament does not forward reports to states.
Courts have no role in this reporting.
POL-8.3.6-Q26.also: The Governor also attaches a memorandum on action taken.

POL-8.3.6-Q27.lead: Summoning power flows from its civil-court powers.

head: Item
Verdict
rows: A: summon and examine on oath

points: Art 338(8) grants civil-court powers during investigation or inquiry.
Summoning and examining on oath is the first listed power.
POL-8.3.6-Q27.also: It can also regulate its own procedure.

POL-8.3.6-Q28.lead: It investigates and recommends; it cannot punish.
points: Discovery of documents is a listed power.
Evidence on affidavits is a listed power.
Requisitioning public records is a listed power.
POL-8.3.6-Q28.also: Issuing summons for witnesses and documents is also listed.

POL-8.3.6-Q29.lead: Art 338(9): Centre and states shall consult NCSC on major SC policies.
points: The duty is mandatory, not optional.
It binds both Union and state governments.

POL-8.3.6-Q30.lead: Clause 10 reads SC references as including Anglo-Indians.
points: OBC role ended in 2018 with the 102nd CAA.
Denotified tribes are not covered by Art 338.
Minorities come under the statutory NCM.

POL-8.3.6-Q31.lead: OBC role ended in 2018, but Anglo-Indian role remains.
points: 1 and 2 are correct: NCBC got Art 338B in 2018.
3 is wrong: Art 338(10) still covers the Anglo-Indian community.

POL-8.3.6-Q32.lead: Social Justice and Empowerment handles SC welfare.
points: Tribal Affairs is nodal for NCST.
Home and Law do not handle SC welfare bodies.

POL-8.3.6-Q33.lead: Same model, different Articles; Kunwar Singh led NCST first.
points: Statement 1: NCSC under 338, NCST under 338A, same design.
Statement 2: Kunwar Singh headed NCST from 2004 to 2007.

POL-8.3.6-Q34.lead: Kishor Makwana assumed charge on 11 March 2024.
points: Vijay Sampla was the previous NCSC Chairperson.
Ram Shankar Katheria headed NCSC earlier (2017-2020).
Antar Singh Arya is linked to the NCST.

POL-8.3.6-Q35.lead: State commissions rest on state laws, not the Constitution.
points: Only national SC, ST and BC commissions are constitutional.
They are backed by state Acts, so not merely advisory.
Art 323B deals with tribunals.
Combined AP SC-ST Commission came in 2003 with statutory status.
Residual AP set up the ST Commission in 2020, then SC Commission in 2021.

POL-8.3.6-Q37.lead: 1+5 members, 3 years, 65 age; appointed by the State.
points: 1 and 3 are correct.
2 is wrong: the State Government appoints them, as it is a statutory state body.
POL-8.3.6-Q37.also: Members must belong to SCs; one woman member is required.

POL-8.3.6-Q38.lead: Overruling Chinnaiah is what opened the way to sub-classification.
points: 7-judge Bench, 6:1, delivered on 1 August 2024.
Justice Bela M. Trivedi dissented, citing Art 341.
It did not change Art 338 or NCSC's structure.

POL-8.3.7-Q01.lead: NCST is created directly by Article 338-A of the Constitution.
points: NCW, NHRC and NCPCR were all created by ordinary Acts of Parliament.
Hence they are statutory, not constitutional, bodies.
POL-8.3.7-Q01.also: NCM is also statutory; NCSC and NCBC are constitutional.

POL-8.3.7-Q02.lead: A body written into the Constitution can be changed only by amendment.

head: Item
Verdict
rows: R: created by the Constitution itself

points: An ordinary law cannot override Article 338-A.
Statutory commissions can be changed by a simple Act of Parliament.

POL-8.3.7-Q03.lead: Part XVI deals with special provisions for certain classes (Arts 330-342A).
points: Part XIV covers services and Public Service Commissions.
Part XV covers elections.
Part XVIII covers emergency provisions.

POL-8.3.7-Q04.lead: Special Officer first; 65th CAA upgraded it to a commission.
points: The Special Officer was known as the Commissioner for SCs and STs.
The combined commission covered both SCs and STs till 2004.

POL-8.3.7-Q05.lead: The 65th CAA took effect on 12 March 1992.
points: 19 February 2004 is when the 89th Amendment took effect.
1990 is the year of enactment, not commencement.
15 August 1993 has no link to this commission.

POL-8.3.7-Q06.lead: Ramdhan headed the combined body; Kunwar Singh the first separate NCST.
points: Suraj Bhan was the first chairman of the separate NCSC (2004-07), not NCST.

POL-8.3.7-Q07.lead: Distinct tribal problems led to a separate ministry in 1999.
points: The same logic later led to splitting the combined commission in 2003.

POL-8.3.7-Q08.lead: 89th CAA split the body: amended 338, inserted 338-A.
points: Art 338-B (NCBC) came only with the 102nd Amendment in 2018.

POL-8.3.7-Q09.lead: 89th CAA took effect on 19 February 2004 (NCST Foundation Day).
points: 12 March 1992 is the 65th Amendment's commencement.
2003 is the year of enactment, not commencement.
2005 relates to the 'other functions' Rules.
Art 338-B created the NCBC, the newest of the three.
Three or four leaves out the Vice-Chairperson or a member.
Seven is not prescribed for NCST.
POL-8.3.7-Q11.also: The NCSC has the same five-member structure.

POL-8.3.7-Q12.lead: President appoints and fixes service conditions; resignation goes to him.
points: Art 338-A(3) lets the President determine conditions of service and tenure by rule.
These are the NCST Rules, 2004.

POL-8.3.7-Q13.lead: NCST members serve three-year terms under the 2004 Rules.
points: Five years is not the NCST term.
'Six years or 65' is the formula for the CEC/UPSC-type posts.
Tenure is fixed by the President, not Parliament.

POL-8.3.7-Q14.lead: The cap is two terms in total, consecutive or not.
points: The rule counts total terms, not consecutive ones.
Parliament has no role in this appointment.

POL-8.3.7-Q15.lead: At least one Member must be a woman.
points: No judicial, parliamentary or regional quota is prescribed.

POL-8.3.7-Q16.lead: Cabinet Minister, Minister of State, Secretary — in that order.
points: Some guides say members have Deputy Minister rank; the official position is Secretary to GoI.

POL-8.3.7-Q17.lead: Ministry of Tribal Affairs is the nodal ministry.
points: MoSJE is nodal for the NCSC, not NCST.
Home and Rural Development have no nodal role here.

POL-8.3.7-Q18.lead: Both separate bodies arose together in 2004.
points: They are mirror bodies: same composition, appointment and tenure.
Only the target community and 'other functions' differ.

POL-8.3.7-Q19.lead: Six functions; reports go to the President, not the PM.
points: The sixth function is the catch-all for President-specified duties.

POL-8.3.7-Q20.lead: Inquiring into specific complaints is an Art 338-A(5) function.
points: Administration and regulations belong to the Governor under the Fifth Schedule.
Delimitation is the Delimitation Commission's work.
POL-8.3.7-Q20.also: Monitoring overall safeguards is a separate, general function.

POL-8.3.7-Q21.lead: NCST is advisory and evaluative, not executive.
points: It neither sanctions funds nor implements schemes.
Budget approval rests with legislatures.

POL-8.3.7-Q22.lead: NCST recommends; government may reject with reasons.
points: Non-acceptance must be explained in a memorandum laid before Parliament.
2003 is the 89th Amendment.
2004 is the tenure Rules and NCST's birth.
2006 is the Forest Rights Act year.

POL-8.3.7-Q24.lead: MFP rights and PESA are listed; ADC administration is not.
points: NCST monitors implementation; it does not run tribal areas.

POL-8.3.7-Q25.lead: Declaring Scheduled Areas is the President's Fifth Schedule power.
points: Land alienation, shifting cultivation and rehabilitation are all in the 2005 list.
Mineral/water rights, livelihoods and social afforestation are the others.

POL-8.3.7-Q26.lead: Report plus action-taken memorandum go to Parliament.
points: This is Art 338-A(6); it mirrors the NCSC rule.

POL-8.3.7-Q27.lead: State-related reports route through the President to the Governor.
points: The Commission reports only to the President, never directly to a CM.
The Governor adds a memorandum on action taken.

POL-8.3.7-Q28.lead: It has civil-court powers of a suit, not criminal punishment.
points: Summons, oath, affidavits, records and discovery of documents are listed in Art 338-A(8).
It cannot convict or sentence anyone.

POL-8.3.7-Q29.lead: Both true, but from separate clauses; R doesn't explain A.
points: Procedure power is a grant of autonomy; civil-court powers aid inquiries.

POL-8.3.7-Q30.lead: Consultation is mandatory; approval is not required.
points: NCST's advice is not a veto.
TAC is a Fifth Schedule body in states with Scheduled Areas.

POL-8.3.7-Q31.lead: NCST monitors; Scheduled Areas are run by Fifth Schedule machinery.
points: Governor, TACs and autonomous councils administer tribal areas.
338-A came via the 89th CAA (2003); 338-B via the 102nd CAA (2018).

POL-8.3.7-Q33.lead: Antar Singh Arya was appointed on 9 March 2024.
points: Kishore Makwana heads the NCSC.
Harsh Chouhan and Rameshwar Oraon are former NCST chairpersons.

POL-8.3.7-Q34.lead: State commissions are statutory; AP ST commission came in 2020.
points: AP's separate SC commission followed in 2021.
The combined AP SC-ST commission dated from 2003.
In AP the ST commission came before the SC commission.

POL-8.3.7-Q36.lead: Five members, one woman, three-year term.
points: Tenure and conditions are set by the President's Rules of 2004.

POL-8.3.7-Q38.lead: Report to President → memorandum → laid before Parliament.
points: The memorandum must accompany the report when it is laid.

POL-8.3.7-Q39.lead: MoSJE handles SC matters; MoTA (1999) handles ST matters.
points: Option 1 reverses the pair.
Home Affairs is not nodal for either commission.

POL-8.3.7-Q40.lead: Investigative, advisory and reporting — not adjudicatory.
points: NCST can inquire and recommend but cannot decide disputes or award damages.

POL-8.3.8-Q01.lead: The 1953 commission was chaired by Kaka Kalelkar.
points: B.P. Mandal headed the second commission (1979).
R.N. Prasad was the first NCBC chairman (1993).
G. Rohini headed the OBC sub-categorisation commission (2017).
1953-55 relates to the Kaka Kalelkar Commission.
1990 is when the Mandal report was implemented by V.P. Singh govt.
1992 is the Indra Sawhney judgment.

POL-8.3.8-Q03.lead: Indra Sawhney (Mandal case, 1992) ordered a permanent statutory body.
points: Balaji (1962) first spoke of a 50% limit.
Jaishri Patil (2021) is the Maratha quota case.
Nagaraj (2006) dealt with SC/ST promotion quotas.

POL-8.3.8-Q04.lead: Parliament passed the NCBC Act, 1993 after the Mandal judgment.
points: The 1955 Act deals with untouchability offences.
There is no NCBC Act, 2018; 2018 brought the Repeal Act.
The 65th CAA made the SC/ST Commission multi-member.
NCSC has been constitutional since 1950 (Art 338).
NCST was split from an already constitutional body in 2003.
The Finance Commission has always been under Art 280.
The 124th Bill became the 103rd CAA (EWS quota).
The 127th Bill became the 105th CAA, 2021.
The 121st Bill became the 99th CAA (NJAC).

POL-8.3.8-Q07.lead: Art 338-B was inserted by the 102nd CAA, 2018.
points: Art 338 is for NCSC.
Art 338-A is for NCST.
Art 340 is for an ad hoc backward classes commission.
The 89th and 102nd are 15 years apart and often swapped.
The 65th CAA replaced the single Special Officer with a multi-member body.

POL-8.3.8-Q09.lead: SEBC definition is in Art 366(26C), not 26B.
points: Clause 26B defines a co-operative society (97th CAA).
Arts 338-B and 342-A were both inserted in 2018.

POL-8.3.8-Q10.lead: Art 342-A mirrors Arts 341/342: consultation with the Governor.
points: The Chief Minister is not named in Art 342-A.
NCBC advises but is not the consulted authority for notification.
The legislature has no role in the presidential notification.

POL-8.3.8-Q11.lead: Art 342-A(2): only Parliament by law can alter the Central List.
points: The President cannot vary the list once notified.
NCBC only examines requests and advises.
Courts do not prepare or amend the list.

POL-8.3.8-Q12.lead: Art 366(26C) was inserted by the 102nd CAA for SEBCs.
points: Clause 24 defines Scheduled Castes.
Clause 25 defines Scheduled Tribes.
Clause 26B defines a co-operative society.

POL-8.3.8-Q13.lead: A separate NCBC (Repeal) Act, 2018 ended the statutory body.
points: The 105th CAA dealt with state SEBC lists.
The 103rd CAA introduced the 10% EWS quota.
No 2011 amendment repealed the Act.

POL-8.3.8-Q14.lead: Constitutional status under 338-B is what makes it equal to NCSC/NCST.
points: All three are now constitutional bodies with similar structure.
Its functions were also enlarged after 2018.

POL-8.3.8-Q15.lead: Social Justice and Empowerment handles OBC/SEBC matters.
points: Tribal Affairs is nodal for NCST.
Minority Affairs is nodal for NCM.
Home Affairs is not the nodal ministry here.

POL-8.3.8-Q16.lead: Five in all: Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, three Members.
points: Same structure as NCSC and NCST.
Other options mix up counts of other commissions.

POL-8.3.8-Q17.lead: Appointment and service conditions are both with the President.
points: Service conditions come from Rules made by the President in 2018, not a Parliament law.

POL-8.3.8-Q18.lead: Three-year term, not more than two terms.
points: 6 years/65 years applies to CAG.
No PM-pleasure tenure exists for NCBC.

POL-8.3.8-Q20.lead: All three are listed functions under Art 338-B(5).
points: These match functions 1, 2 and 3 of the six listed.

POL-8.3.8-Q21.lead: Reports go to the President, annually and as needed.
points: The President then lays them before Parliament.
Neither the Speaker nor a Minister receives them directly.

POL-8.3.8-Q22.lead: Reporting is annual and ad hoc, not five-yearly.
points: Annual and special reports are both allowed.
Reports cover the working of safeguards.

POL-8.3.8-Q23.lead: The President can specify further functions for SEBCs.
points: Recommendations for Union and state measures are a core function.
Clause 5(f) lets the President assign other functions.

POL-8.3.8-Q24.lead: An action-taken memorandum with reasons for rejection is required.
points: CAG and Attorney General have no role here.
Cabinet approval is not a stated requirement.

POL-8.3.8-Q25.lead: Art 338-B(7) says 'forwarded to the State Government'.
points: By contrast, NCSC and NCST reports concerning a state go to the Governor (Arts 338(7), 338-A(7)).
The State Government lays it before the state legislature with a memorandum on action taken.

POL-8.3.8-Q27.lead: NCBC has civil court powers for inquiry, not punishment.
points: Summons, documents, affidavits and public records are listed powers.
It cannot sentence anyone to imprisonment.
The Central List is changed only by Parliament.
Members are appointed by the President.

POL-8.3.8-Q29.lead: Consultation is mandatory on all major SEBC policy matters.
points: The scope is not limited to recruitment or budgets.
Delimitation is unrelated to NCBC.

POL-8.3.8-Q30.lead: Jaishri Patil (5 May 2021) triggered the 105th CAA.
points: Indra Sawhney (1992) set the 50% ceiling.
Janhit Abhiyan (2022) upheld the EWS quota.
Davinder Singh (2024) allowed SC sub-classification.

POL-8.3.8-Q31.lead: The Court upheld the 102nd CAA but interpreted 342-A narrowly.
points: It did not strike down Art 342-A; it read it as excluding state power (3:2).
The quota failed the Indra Sawhney 50% limit.
102nd created 338-B and 342-A.
103rd gave the EWS quota.
104th extended SC/ST seat reservation and ended Anglo-Indian nomination.

POL-8.3.8-Q33.lead: All three are correct; assent came on 18 August 2021.
points: Clause 342-A(3) lets states keep their own SEBC lists.
338-B(9) and 366(26C) were adjusted to match.

POL-8.3.8-Q34.lead: The 105th CAA exempts states from NCBC consultation for state lists.
points: Presidential notification and Parliament's law apply to the Central List only.
NCBC's advice is not binding.
Art 340 commissions include Kalelkar, Mandal and Rohini.
Art 342-A copies the 341/342 pattern for SEBCs.

POL-8.3.8-Q37.lead: Justice R.N. Prasad headed NCBC from 1993 to 1996.
points: K. Puttaswamy was the first AP BC Commission chairman.
Ahir became chairperson in 2022.
G. Rohini headed the sub-categorisation commission.

POL-8.3.8-Q38.lead: Sadhvi Niranjan Jyoti took charge on 18 March 2026.
points: Ahir was chairperson from December 2022.
Bhagwan Lal Sahni was the first chair after constitutional status (2019).
Kiran Mahalle joined as a Member.
Bill: April 2017.
105th CAA assent: August 2021.
Ahir: December 2022; Jyoti: March 2026.

POL-8.3.8-Q40.lead: It studied sub-categorisation within the Central OBC list.
points: Creamy layer limits are revised by DoPT.
Promotion quotas concern SCs/STs (Art 16(4A)).
EWS came by the 103rd CAA.

POL-8.3.8-Q41.lead: All three statements on the Rohini Commission are correct.
points: Headed by former Delhi HC Chief Justice G. Rohini.
Report not yet officially made public.

POL-8.3.8-Q42.lead: AP BC Commission is statutory, set up by a 1993 state Act.
points: Only the national commission has constitutional status.
State government both appoints and can remove members.

POL-8.3.8-Q43.lead: The chairman must be a former HC or SC judge.
points: Other members need expertise in BC matters.
Its first chairman was Justice K. Puttaswamy.
Consultation on list changes is the state commission's key role.
Puttaswamy chaired it from 1994 to 2000.

POL-8.3.8-Q45.lead: B.S. Ramulu was the first Telangana BC Commission chairman.
points: G. Niranjan became chairman in 2024.
Puttaswamy chaired the AP commission.
R.N. Prasad was the first NCBC chairman.
The 1992 judgment led to the 1993 Act.
The 2021 judgment came after the 2018 amendment it interpreted.

POL-8.3.8-Q47.lead: Only the SC body traces back to 1950; NCBC became constitutional in 2018.
points: Composition, tenure and civil-court powers are identical for all three.
NCST became separate in 2003.

POL-8.3.8-Q48.lead: Denial of benefits is a complaint of deprivation of rights.
points: Notifying the list is the President's role.
Laying reports and fixing service conditions are also the President's tasks.

POL-8.3.9-Q01.lead: Article 350B was a 1956 addition, not original.
points: The 7th Amendment implemented the States Reorganisation scheme.
It placed Art 350B in Part XVII.

POL-8.3.9-Q02.lead: The SRC (1953-55) felt minorities in new linguistic States needed a watchdog.
points: The Dhar Commission (1948) and JVP Committee (1948-49) opposed linguistic States.
The Official Language Commission (1955, B.G. Kher) dealt with Hindi.
POL-8.3.9-Q02.also: SRC was chaired by Fazl Ali.

POL-8.3.9-Q03.lead: Part XVII (Arts 343-351) deals with Official Language.
points: Part III has Fundamental Rights including Arts 29-30.
Part XVI has special provisions for certain classes (SC/ST).
Part XVIII has emergency provisions.

POL-8.3.9-Q04.lead: Both came in 1956; 350A is about mother-tongue instruction.
points: Art 350A: primary-stage instruction in mother tongue.
Art 350B: Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities.

POL-8.3.9-Q05.lead: The President appoints and fixes reporting intervals.
points: The Minority Affairs Minister only routes the reports.
No annual interval is fixed by the Constitution itself.

POL-8.3.9-Q06.lead: Art 350B(2): reports go to both Houses and the State Governments.
points: The Supreme Court has no role in these reports.
The NCM is a separate statutory body (1992 Act).

POL-8.3.9-Q07.lead: Art 350B states only appointment and duties.
points: Tenure, removal, qualifications, salary and service conditions are all left unspecified.
This contrasts with the CAG and CEC, whose removal is spelt out.

POL-8.3.9-Q08.lead: No constitutional removal procedure means no tenure security.
points: The CAG can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge (Art 148).
The Special Officer's terms are set administratively.

POL-8.3.9-Q09.lead: Art 350B came in 1956; the office was set up in 1957.
points: 1956 is the year of the 7th Amendment, not of the office.
1950 is commencement of the Constitution.
POL-8.3.9-Q09.also: The officer is called the Commissioner for Linguistic Minorities (CLM).

POL-8.3.9-Q10.lead: HQ moved back from Allahabad to New Delhi in 2015.
points: Allahabad was the HQ earlier; older books still print it.
Kolkata and Chennai are regional offices.
The office did not start at Allahabad.
Answer 'Allahabad' for current HQ is outdated.
Each regional office is headed by an Assistant Commissioner.
There is no regional office in Andhra Pradesh.

POL-8.3.9-Q13.lead: The three regional offices are Belgaum, Chennai and Kolkata.
points: Hyderabad has no CLM office.
The HQ is at New Delhi.

POL-8.3.9-Q14.lead: Regional offices are headed by Assistant Commissioners.
points: The Deputy Commissioner sits at headquarters.
Three regional offices exist.

POL-8.3.9-Q15.lead: All three describe how the CLM works on the ground.
points: Grievances can come from individuals, groups or organisations.
The CLM also discusses with Governors, CMs and Chief Secretaries.

POL-8.3.9-Q16.lead: CLM is under the Ministry of Minority Affairs.
points: Home Affairs is a common wrong choice.
Education and Culture ministries have no supervisory role.
POL-8.3.9-Q16.also: Reports reach the President through the Union Minority Affairs Minister.

POL-8.3.9-Q17.lead: Reports are routed via the Union Minority Affairs Minister.
points: The CLM does not submit directly in practice.
The Speaker receives it only after the President lays it before Parliament.

POL-8.3.9-Q18.lead: The CLM monitors and reports; it has no decree powers.
points: Questionnaires, visits, conferences, seminars, meetings and review are its tools.
It is not a quasi-judicial body.

POL-8.3.9-Q19.lead: Investigate and report are functions; awareness and grievances are objectives.
points: 3 functions: investigate, report, monitor.
4 objectives: equal opportunity, awareness, effective implementation, grievance redress.

POL-8.3.9-Q20.lead: Mission: get every State/UT to implement the safeguards.
points: Minority status is decided State-wise, not nationally.
Census is by the Registrar General; Eighth Schedule changes need an amendment.

POL-8.3.9-Q21.lead: Mother tongue differing from the State majority decides minority status.
points: The same language can be majority in one State and minority in another.
Eighth Schedule listing is irrelevant to minority status.

POL-8.3.9-Q22.lead: 29 conserve culture; 30 institutions; 347 recognition; 350 grievance language.
points: Art 350A adds mother-tongue primary education.
Art 350B creates the Special Officer to watch over all these.

POL-8.3.9-Q23.lead: Art 30(1) is the direct source of the right in A.
points: Art 30 is a Fundamental Right in Part III.
It covers both religious and linguistic minorities.

POL-8.3.9-Q24.lead: Art 347 acts 'on a demand being made in that behalf'.
points: No Parliament resolution or court consent is needed.
The CLM only investigates; it does not trigger Art 347.
It is a general language right, useful to minorities.
It sits in Part XVII with Arts 350A and 350B.

POL-8.3.9-Q26.lead: Art 350A covers primary-stage instruction in the mother tongue.
points: Art 29(2) bars denial of admission on grounds like language.
Art 45 is early childhood care; Art 351 is development of Hindi.
POL-8.3.9-Q26.also: The President may issue directions to States under Art 350A.

POL-8.3.9-Q27.lead: Minorities are recognised but 'minority' is not defined.
points: Art 30 refers to minorities 'based on religion or language'.
Religious minorities are notified under the NCM Act, 1992.

POL-8.3.9-Q28.lead: Reports go to the President, not the Governors.
points: State Governments receive copies sent by the President.
Governors are only consulted during CLM visits.
The office followed the Article by a year.
The original Constitution had no such officer.

POL-8.3.9-Q30.lead: Ministry is Minority Affairs; HQ is New Delhi since 2015.
points: Older notes still print Allahabad as HQ.
Other regional offices: Belgaum, Chennai.

POL-8.4.1-Q01.lead: NHRC is a statutory body under the PHRA, 1993.
points: Art 338 creates the NCSC, a constitutional body.
PCR Act, 1955 deals with untouchability offences.
The 1952 Act is used for ad hoc inquiry commissions.
POL-8.4.1-Q01.also: The PHRA was amended in 2006 and 2019.

POL-8.4.1-Q02.lead: Paris 1991, Ordinance Sep 1993, NHRC Oct 1993, assent Jan 1994.
points: Paris workshop: October 1991.
Ordinance: 28 September 1993.
NHRC constituted: 12 October 1993.
Act assented: 8 January 1994, deemed in force from 28 September 1993.

POL-8.4.1-Q03.lead: Paris Principles (1991) govern national human rights institutions.
points: Paris Principles were endorsed by the UN General Assembly on 20 December 1993.
Vienna Declaration (1993) is a world conference outcome, not NHRI standards.
Geneva Conventions concern humanitarian law in armed conflict.

POL-8.4.1-Q04.lead: The definition covers Constitution and enforceable covenant rights.
points: Statement 3 is wrong: covenant-based rights enforceable in India are also covered.

POL-8.4.1-Q05.lead: NHRC has no power to punish; it supplements, not replaces, courts.
points: The first three are the three stated objectives.
NHRC is often called the 'watchdog' of human rights.
No Article of the Constitution creates NHRC.
It was created by an Act, not an executive order.
Its recommendations are not binding.
9 would be the pre-2019 count of 1+4+4 (two HR members then).
11 or 15 match no version of the Act.
'Only a retired CJI' was the pre-2019 rule.
HC Chief Justice qualifies only as a member (or SHRC chair).
No 'eminent jurist' route exists.

POL-8.4.1-Q09.lead: Chair from CJI/SC; one SC judge, one HC CJ, three HR experts.
points: At least one of the three human-rights members must be a woman.

POL-8.4.1-Q10.lead: 2019 Amendment: three such members, at least one woman.
points: The Act prescribes no caste, civil-service or NGO-nomination condition.
Before 2019 there were only two such members.

POL-8.4.1-Q11.lead: CVC is an anti-corruption body, not a deemed member.
points: The seven deemed members: NCM, NCSC, NCST, NCW, NCBC, NCPCR chairs and CCPD.
The first three in the options were added in 2019.
Ex-officio rose from 4 (NCM, NCSC, NCST, NCW) to 7.
Tenure cut to 3 years or age 70.

POL-8.4.1-Q13.lead: Pre-2019 deemed members: NCM, NCSC, NCST, NCW.
points: NCBC and NCPCR chairs, and CCPD, were added only in 2019.

POL-8.4.1-Q14.lead: President appoints by warrant under hand and seal.
points: The PM only heads the recommending committee.
The CJI is consulted only for sitting judges.
The Home Minister is a committee member.

POL-8.4.1-Q15.lead: The CJI is not on the six-member committee.
points: Members: PM, LS Speaker, RS Deputy Chairman, two LoPs, Home Minister.
Note: RS Deputy Chairman, not the Vice-President/RS Chairman.

POL-8.4.1-Q16.lead: The Prime Minister heads the six-member committee.
points: Speaker is a member, not chair.
Vice-President and Law Minister are not members.

POL-8.4.1-Q17.lead: Parliament has no role in approving appointments.
points: The CJI-consultation safeguard applies only to sitting judges/HC Chief Justices.

POL-8.4.1-Q18.lead: Sitting judge/HC CJ: CJI must be consulted first.
points: No Governor, parliamentary or collegium approval is prescribed.

POL-8.4.1-Q19.lead: 2019 cut tenure to 3 years or 70, whichever is earlier.
points: 5 years/70 was the pre-2019 rule.
6 years/65 is the CEC/CAG pattern, not NHRC.

POL-8.4.1-Q20.lead: 2019 removed the one-more-term cap on re-appointment.
points: Statement 2 describes the pre-2019 position, which was removed.
The post-office employment bar protects independence.

POL-8.4.1-Q21.lead: SC inquiry is needed only for misbehaviour or incapacity.
points: The five objective grounds allow direct removal by the President.
Statement 4 is a common error; Sec 5 separates the two routes.

POL-8.4.1-Q22.lead: Misbehaviour needs SC inquiry and advice.
points: The other three are among the five direct grounds.
Insolvency and outside paid employment complete the five.

POL-8.4.1-Q23.lead: Removal is by President after SC inquiry; Parliament has no role.
points: The process mirrors SC-judge removal in substance but uses a Presidential reference.
No impeachment motion exists for NHRC members.

POL-8.4.1-Q24.lead: Salaries are prescribed by the Central Government.
points: Statement 2 is wrong: the Central Government, not a Schedule, fixes salaries.
Protection of service conditions secures independence.
The Chairperson heads the Commission but is not its CEO.
The DG heads the investigation wing.

POL-8.4.1-Q26.lead: Three routes: suo motu, petition, court order.
points: The other options wrongly restrict NHRC to a single route.
It also covers negligence of a public servant in preventing violation.

POL-8.4.1-Q27.lead: NHRC cannot quash orders; it only recommends or approaches courts.
points: Statement 3 would need a writ court; NHRC can only petition SC/HC.

POL-8.4.1-Q28.lead: Procedure law is made by Parliament, not NHRC.
points: The first three are listed functions.
Research and human-rights literacy are also its functions.

POL-8.4.1-Q29.lead: Listed among NHRC functions in Sec 12.
points: CIC handles RTI appeals.
Law Commission recommends law reform.
Inter-State Council handles Centre-state coordination.

POL-8.4.1-Q30.lead: Headquartered in Delhi; may set up offices elsewhere.
points: It regulates its own procedure.
It can hold camp sittings across the country.

POL-8.4.1-Q31.lead: Inquiry powers are court-like; punishment powers are absent.
points: Its proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings.
It can only recommend prosecution.

POL-8.4.1-Q32.lead: Judicial character applies to inquiry, not to relief.
points: Only its summoning/inquiry power is court-like.
Its recommendations are not binding.

POL-8.4.1-Q33.lead: It may utilise government officers or agencies for investigation.
points: It cannot direct prosecution itself.
Closing a complaint for staff shortage is not a statutory option.

POL-8.4.1-Q34.lead: Sec 36(2): no inquiry after one year from the act.
points: The one-year bar applies to all complaints.
There is no SC-leave exception or mandatory transfer.

POL-8.4.1-Q35.lead: NHRC has no power to attach property.
points: Interim relief can also be recommended.
Approaching SC/HC is its only direct court-facing step.

POL-8.4.1-Q36.lead: NHRC recommends relief; it cannot grant it or punish.
points: Statements 2 and 3 confuse recommendation with enforcement.

POL-8.4.1-Q37.lead: Sec 18(e): action taken to be reported within one month.
points: Three months applies only to armed forces cases.
15 days and six months are not prescribed.

POL-8.4.1-Q38.lead: The action-taken duty gives non-binding advice real weight.
points: Recommendations are not binding, yet they must be answered.
Reasons for non-acceptance also go before the legislature.

POL-8.4.1-Q39.lead: Sec 19: limited role—report from Centre, then recommend.
points: Centre must report action within three months here.
It is not barred entirely, but cannot investigate directly.

POL-8.4.1-Q40.lead: General one month; armed forces three months.
points: Some books wrongly give three months for all cases.

POL-8.4.1-Q41.lead: Reasons for non-acceptance must accompany the report.
points: Statement 3 is wrong; this is a key accountability check.

POL-8.4.1-Q42.lead: Manpower shortage has persisted since inception.
points: The SC in 2017 directed the Government to fix the staff shortage.
It handles about one lakh complaints a year.

POL-8.4.1-Q43.lead: Paris Principles require financial and staff autonomy for NHRIs.
points: UDHR (10 Dec 1948) lists rights, not NHRI standards.
Bangalore Principles concern judges' conduct.

POL-8.4.1-Q44.lead: MHA is the nodal ministry and releases NHRC's grants.
points: Law Ministry is a common distractor but is not the nodal ministry.
Social Justice handles NCSC/NCBC matters.

POL-8.4.1-Q45.lead: Sec 36(1): no inquiry into matters pending before another Commission.
points: Media reports allow suo motu action.
Relatives' complaints and bonded labour are within its mandate.

POL-8.4.1-Q46.lead: Recent custodial violence is a core NHRC matter.
points: Sub judice, service and time-barred matters are excluded.
Vague or anonymous complaints are also not entertained.

POL-8.4.1-Q47.lead: Delhi's human-rights functions stay with NHRC.
points: Other UTs' functions may be conferred on an SHRC by the Centre.

POL-8.4.1-Q48.lead: 2019 widened both posts to ordinary judges.
points: Earlier SHRC chair had to be a former HC Chief Justice only.

POL-8.4.1-Q49.lead: Arun Kumar Mishra (2021) followed the 2019 change.
points: Ranganath Misra (first chair, 1993), Balakrishnan and Dattu were former CJIs.

POL-8.4.1-Q50.lead: He was a former SC judge, never CJI.
points: He succeeded Justice Arun Kumar Mishra, whose 3-year term ended on 1 June 2024.
HC Chief Justice qualifies only for a member seat.

POL-8.4.1-Q51.lead: State notifies a Court of Session with HC Chief Justice's concurrence.
points: A special public prosecutor is appointed for each such court.
Munsiff and CJM courts are lower-tier courts.

POL-8.4.1-Q52.lead: Camp sittings and open hearings are NHRC outreach tools.
points: Lok Adalats are under Legal Services Authorities.
Gram Nyayalayas are village-level courts under a 2008 Act.
POL-8.4.1-Q52.also: Complaints include custodial deaths, torture, fake encounters and bonded labour.

POL-8.4.1-Q53.lead: Being statutory, it can be changed by ordinary amendment.
points: The 2006 and 2019 amendments were ordinary Acts.
No constitutional amendment is needed.

POL-8.4.2-Q01.lead: The PHR Act 1993 creates both NHRC and SHRCs.
points: The 1955 Act deals with untouchability offences.
The 1952 Act is for ad hoc inquiry commissions.
No separate Human Rights Courts Act exists; courts are under the 1993 Act.

POL-8.4.2-Q02.lead: SHRC is statutory and optional; the Act says a state 'may' constitute it.
points: 1 is correct: it is not a constitutional body.
2 is wrong: unlike SPSC (Art 315), it is not compulsory.
3 is correct: PHR Act 1993 is a Central Act.

POL-8.4.2-Q03.lead: The Act leaves the location to state government notification.
points: No capital or High Court seat is fixed by the Act.
NHRC has no role in fixing SHRC headquarters.
AP SHRC, for example, is located at Kurnool, not Amaravati.

POL-8.4.2-Q04.lead: SHRC is a three-member body: Chairperson plus two members.
points: Four members was the pre-2006 strength.
Five members plus ex-officio members describes the NHRC.
SHRC has no Vice-Chairperson.
The Act was passed in 1993.
The 2006 Amendment cut SHRC members from four to two.
The 2019 Amendment cut tenure from five to three years.

POL-8.4.2-Q06.lead: Chairperson comes from High Court level: ex-CJ or a HC Judge.
points: Ex-CJI qualifies for NHRC, not SHRC.
A District Judge (7 yrs) qualifies only as a member.
A human rights expert can be a member, not Chairperson.

POL-8.4.2-Q07.lead: Both are 2019 changes, but tenure does not explain eligibility.
points: A is true: 'or a Judge of a HC' was added in 2019.
R is true but concerns tenure, not who can be Chairperson.

POL-8.4.2-Q08.lead: District Judge of the state with at least 7 years' experience.
points: 5 years is not prescribed.
10 years is the HC judge eligibility under Art 217 for advocates.
12 years has no basis here.

POL-8.4.2-Q09.lead: The woman-member rule applies to NHRC, not SHRC.
points: 1 and 2 describe the two SHRC member seats.
The 2019 woman-member rule covers NHRC's human rights experts only.

POL-8.4.2-Q10.lead: Governor appoints by warrant under hand and seal.
points: President appoints NHRC members and removes SHRC members.
CM only heads the recommending committee.
HC Chief Justice is consulted only for sitting judges.

POL-8.4.2-Q11.lead: The committee is political-executive; HC Chief Justice is not in it.
points: CM heads the committee.
Speaker and LoP in Assembly are members.
State Home Minister is the fourth member.

POL-8.4.2-Q12.lead: Four core members plus Council Chairman and Council LoP.
points: 4 is the strength in unicameral states.
Council adds exactly two members, so 5 and 7 are wrong.
Andhra Pradesh, having a Council, has a 6-member committee.

POL-8.4.2-Q13.lead: CM heads; Council Chairman is added only where a Council exists.
points: Home Minister sits in every state committee.
Council Chairman cannot be a member where no Council exists.

POL-8.4.2-Q14.lead: Consultation protects judicial independence when serving judges are drawn.
points: Experts and retired judges need no such consultation.
The Secretary is an officer, not a member.

POL-8.4.2-Q15.lead: After 2019: 3 years or age 70, whichever earlier.
points: 5 years/70 was the pre-2019 rule.
6 years/65 resembles CAG/ECI terms.
65 is not the SHRC age limit.
2 is the reverse of the truth: they are eligible for reappointment.

POL-8.4.2-Q17.lead: Post-tenure bar covers both state and Central government employment.
points: Reappointment is allowed after 2019.
The Act bars only government employment, not private activity.

POL-8.4.2-Q18.lead: Resignation goes to the appointing authority, the Governor.
points: President removes but does not receive resignation.
CM and NHRC Chairperson have no such role.

POL-8.4.2-Q19.lead: Governor appoints, but only the President removes.
points: Governor has no removal power.
The legislature plays no role in removal.
HC Chief Justice is not a removing authority.

POL-8.4.2-Q20.lead: R directly explains why the Governor cannot remove.
points: Same appointer/remover split as the State PSC.

POL-8.4.2-Q21.lead: Misbehaviour needs a Supreme Court inquiry first.
points: Insolvency, unsound mind and imprisonment need no SC inquiry.
Paid outside employment and infirmity are the other direct grounds.

POL-8.4.2-Q22.lead: Misbehaviour/incapacity removal needs SC inquiry and advice.
points: Governor's consent is not required.
No legislative resolution is involved.
NHRC has no role in SHRC removal.

POL-8.4.2-Q23.lead: Section 26 of the Act: as prescribed by the state government.
points: Central government fixes NHRC salaries.
Parliament does not fix them directly.
NHRC has no such power.
POL-8.4.2-Q23.also: These cannot be varied to their disadvantage after appointment.

POL-8.4.2-Q24.lead: SHRC is confined to Lists II and III of the Seventh Schedule.
points: Union List matters are beyond SHRC.
All three Lists describes the NHRC's reach.

POL-8.4.2-Q25.lead: SHRC cannot inquire into a matter already before NHRC or another statutory commission.
points: Parallel inquiries are barred to avoid conflicting findings.
SHRC cannot take over NHRC cases.

POL-8.4.2-Q26.lead: Defence is a Union subject; armed forces lie outside SHRC.
points: Seeking a report from the Centre is NHRC's power.
NHRC does have a limited role, so option 4 is wrong.

POL-8.4.2-Q27.lead: UT conferment came in 2019, with Delhi kept under NHRC.
points: 3 is wrong: it was added by the 2019 Amendment.

POL-8.4.2-Q28.lead: All three routes can start an SHRC inquiry.
points: It also covers negligence in preventing a violation.

POL-8.4.2-Q29.lead: Jail visits with recommendations are an SHRC function.
points: SHRC cannot punish anyone.
Treaties are a Union matter.
It can only recommend action, not dismiss.

POL-8.4.2-Q30.lead: Legislation is the legislature's job, not SHRC's.
points: Literacy, NGO support and review of terrorism are listed functions.
It may review safeguards and recommend, but not legislate.

POL-8.4.2-Q31.lead: Research is common to both commissions' function lists.
points: Only the treaty-study function is NHRC-exclusive.

POL-8.4.2-Q32.lead: Treaties are a Union subject, so SHRC has 9 functions vs NHRC's 10.
points: Court intervention, jail visits and NGO support are common to both.
Civil-court powers include summons and taking evidence.

POL-8.4.2-Q34.lead: It can seek reports from the state government and its subordinate authorities.
points: Seeking reports from the Centre on armed forces is an NHRC power.
Courts and NHRC are not its reporting authorities.

POL-8.4.2-Q35.lead: SHRC cannot inquire after one year from the alleged violation.
points: There is a fixed one-year limitation.
No Governor permission route exists.
NHRC is bound by the same one-year rule.

POL-8.4.2-Q36.lead: All three are post-inquiry steps open to SHRC.
points: It may also recommend immediate interim relief.

POL-8.4.2-Q37.lead: Being recommendatory, it can only ask the government to pay.
points: It cannot punish violators either.
Its recommendations do not bind the government.

POL-8.4.2-Q38.lead: Only the one-month action-taken rule is correct.
points: 1 is wrong: recommendations are not binding.
3 is wrong: SHRC has no power to punish.

POL-8.4.2-Q39.lead: State government lays them before the state legislature with an action-taken memorandum.
points: Parliament receives NHRC reports.
The memorandum also gives reasons for rejecting any recommendation.

POL-8.4.2-Q40.lead: A Sessions Court is specified per district for speedy trial of human rights offences.
points: Magistrate, Family Court and Lok Adalat are not named.

POL-8.4.2-Q41.lead: Concurrence of the state High Court's Chief Justice is required.
points: Governor, SHRC and CJI have no role here.
Same CJ-of-HC check appears for sitting judges joining SHRC.

POL-8.4.2-Q42.lead: An advocate of at least 7 years' standing.
points: Alternatively a public prosecutor may be specified.
5, 10 and 15 years are not prescribed.

POL-8.4.2-Q43.lead: Appointer and salary differ; removal by President is common.
points: SHRC has no ex-officio members.
SHRC salary is fixed by the state government.

POL-8.4.2-Q44.lead: Subject-matter jurisdiction is a genuine difference.
points: Both have 3-year tenure after 2019.
Both are statutory under the 1993 Act.
Both have a one-year limitation period.

POL-8.4.2-Q45.lead: SHRC Secretary got these powers, paralleling NHRC's Secretary-General.
points: Chief Secretary and Home Secretary are outside the Commission.
Members do not hold administrative control.

POL-8.4.2-Q46.lead: Justice Subhashan Reddy headed it from 2005 to 2010.
points: K. Punnaiah was first chair of AP SC/ST Commission.
Seetharama Murti headed residual AP SHRC from 2021.
Shameem Akther heads Telangana SHRC.

POL-8.4.2-Q47.lead: Ramasubramanian heads NHRC; Akther heads Telangana SHRC.
points: Seetharama Murti's AP SHRC term ended in March 2024.
AP SHRC chair has remained vacant since then, as last reported.

POL-8.4.2-Q48.lead: Justice Ranganath Misra was the first (1993-1996).
points: Venkatachaliah was second, Verma third, Anand fourth.

POL-8.4.2-Q49.lead: Governor appoints, state government pays, President removes.
points: Central government fixes NHRC salary, not SHRC.
Governor never removes SHRC members.

POL-8.5.1-Q01.lead: RTI flows from freedom of speech and expression, Art 19(1)(a).
points: Art 14 is equality before law.
Art 21A is right to education.
Art 32 is the remedy to move the Supreme Court.
POL-8.5.1-Q01.also: The Constitution does not name RTI expressly.

POL-8.5.1-Q02.lead: Raj Narain (1975) first linked the right to know with Art 19(1)(a).
points: Gopalan (1950) concerned preventive detention.
Bela Banerjee (1954) concerned compensation for acquisition.
Golaknath (1967) concerned amending Fundamental Rights.
Sweden's Freedom of the Press Act, 1766 is the world's first.
USA's Freedom of Information Act came in 1966, before Norway's 1970 law.

POL-8.5.1-Q04.lead: Sweden did so through its Freedom of the Press Act, 1766.
points: Finland followed in 1951.
USA passed its FOIA in 1966.
UK's Freedom of Information Act is of 2000.

POL-8.5.1-Q05.lead: Medha Patkar is known for the Narmada Bachao Andolan.
points: Aruna Roy led MKSS's RTI campaign in Rajasthan.
Sandeep Pandey and Arvind Kejriwal are Magsaysay awardees in the movement.
Dr Jayaprakash Narayan founded Lok Satta.

POL-8.5.1-Q06.lead: Tamil Nadu was first in 1997; Goa followed the same year.
points: Rajasthan and Karnataka acted in 2000.
Delhi (2001) and Maharashtra (2002/2003) came later.

POL-8.5.1-Q07.lead: 15 June 2005 is the assent date; full force came on 12 Oct 2005.
points: Section 31 repealed the 2002 Act.
Statement 2 confuses Presidential assent with full commencement.

POL-8.5.1-Q08.lead: The whole Act became operative on 12 October 2005.
points: 15 June 2005 is the date of Presidential assent.
Some sections (like PIO designation) began earlier, within 120 days of enactment.
POL-8.5.1-Q08.also: 12 October is observed as the RTI anniversary.

POL-8.5.1-Q09.lead: The Act has 6 chapters, 31 sections and 2 Schedules.
points: Section 31 is the last section (repeal of FOI Act 2002).

POL-8.5.1-Q10.lead: Proactive disclosure under Sec 4 directly serves transparency.
points: A is Sec 4(1)(b) suo motu disclosure.
R states the Act's objective, which is why Sec 4 exists, so R explains A.

POL-8.5.1-Q11.lead: Private-body data counts only if a public authority can access it by law.
points: E-mails, samples, models, opinions and advices are expressly listed in Sec 2(f).
Sec 2(f) covers private-body data accessible to a public authority under any law.

POL-8.5.1-Q12.lead: Sec 2(j) covers inspection, notes, copies, samples and electronic data.
points: Citizens may also take notes, extracts and certified copies.

POL-8.5.1-Q13.lead: Sec 3 gives the right to 'all citizens'.
points: Foreigners resident in India are not covered as of right.
A company is not a citizen; it may apply only through a citizen.

POL-8.5.1-Q14.lead: Sec 4(1)(b) requires suo motu publication of such details.
points: Sec 6 deals with filing a request.
Sec 8 lists exemptions.
Sec 19 deals with appeals.

POL-8.5.1-Q15.lead: Sec 6(2) says no reason need be given.
points: Statement 1 is wrong: no reason is required.
Statements 2 and 3 follow Sec 6(1) and 6(2).

POL-8.5.1-Q16.lead: Five days are added when the APIO receives it: 30 + 5 = 35.
points: 30 days applies when the PIO receives it directly.
40 days applies when third-party information is involved.
45 days is the outer limit for deciding a first appeal.
24 hours and 72 hours are not in the Act.
7 days has no basis; normal requests get 30 days.
The APIO route adds 5 days.
Third-party cases need time for notice and representation, so 40 days.

POL-8.5.1-Q20.lead: Second appeal goes to the CIC/SIC, not the High Court.
points: Sec 19(1): first appeal within 30 days to a senior officer.
Sec 19(3): second appeal within 90 days to the Commission.
High Court writ jurisdiction is separate, not an appeal under the Act.

POL-8.5.1-Q21.lead: Sec 19(3) allows 90 days from the first-appeal decision.
points: 30 days is the time for the first appeal.
45 days is the extended time for deciding the first appeal.

POL-8.5.1-Q22.lead: Application, deemed refusal, first appeal, then second appeal.
points: Non-reply in 30 days is a deemed refusal allowing first appeal.
The Commission is the last statutory stage.

POL-8.5.1-Q24.lead: The Act provides fine and disciplinary action only, no jail.
points: A is false: Sec 20 contains no imprisonment.
R correctly states Sec 20(1) and 20(2).
POL-8.5.1-Q24.also: Some guidebooks wrongly add imprisonment; check the Act's text.

POL-8.5.1-Q26.lead: DPDP Act 2023, not the 2019 amendment, rewrote Sec 8(1)(j).
points: Sec 44(3) took effect when DPDP Rules were notified on 14 Nov 2025.
The 2019 amendment dealt only with term and salary of Commissioners.
POL-8.5.1-Q26.also: The general public-interest override in Sec 8(2) still remains.

POL-8.5.1-Q27.lead: The 20-year rule opens old records, with a few exceptions.
points: Exceptions include sovereignty/security, legislative privilege and Cabinet-paper conditions.
10, 15 and 25 years are not in Sec 8(3).

POL-8.5.1-Q28.lead: Sec 24 excludes them, with corruption and human-rights exceptions.
points: Human-rights information needs CIC approval and is given within 45 days.
CRPF, BSF, DRI and ED are also listed.

POL-8.5.1-Q29.lead: Purely private bodies are outside Sec 2(h).
points: Bodies under the Constitution, Parliament/State law or notification are covered.
Substantially financed NGOs are expressly included.

POL-8.5.1-Q30.lead: Decided on 13 Nov 2019 by a bench led by CJI Ranjan Gogoi.
points: Puttaswamy (2017) declared privacy a Fundamental Right.
Raj Narain (1975) linked the right to know with Art 19(1)(a).
Anuradha Bhasin (2020) concerned internet shutdowns.

POL-8.5.1-Q31.lead: The Court balanced RTI with privacy; neither is absolute.
points: Statement 2 is wrong: the Court called RTI and privacy two sides of one coin.
It said Sec 8(1)(j) exists to balance privacy and public interest.
Whistle Blowers Bill came in 2010 and became law in 2014.
DPDP Act, 2023 later amended Sec 8(1)(j) of RTI.
The override applies notwithstanding the Official Secrets Act, 1923.
It is distinct from the personal-information clause 8(1)(j).

POL-8.5.1-Q46.lead: After the J&K Reorganisation Act 2019, the central Act applies.
points: The J&K RTI Act, 2009 was repealed in 2019.
Appeals now go to the Central Information Commission for the UT.

POL-8.5.1-Q47.lead: Tamil Nadu, not Kerala, was first (1997).
points: Aruna Roy led the MKSS campaign in Rajasthan.

POL-8.5.1-Q48.lead: First appeal goes to the First Appellate Authority within 30 days.
points: The Commission hears the second appeal.
The Collector or High Court is not the statutory first appellate forum.

POL-8.5.2-Q01.lead: CIC owes its existence to the RTI Act, 2005, not the Constitution.
points: Art 324 creates the Election Commission.
Art 338 creates the National Commission for SCs.
CIC was set up by statute, not by a mere Cabinet resolution like the old CVC.
POL-8.5.2-Q01.also: Parliament can abolish CIC simply by amending or repealing the RTI Act.

POL-8.5.2-Q02.lead: One Chief plus not more than ten ICs — maximum 11.
points: The same ceiling of ten applies to every State Information Commission.
Only a ceiling is fixed; there is no minimum number.

POL-8.5.2-Q03.lead: Committee: PM, LoP (Lok Sabha), PM-nominated Union Cabinet Minister.
points: No judge sits on the CIC selection committee.
The third member is a Union Cabinet Minister chosen by the PM.

POL-8.5.2-Q04.lead: President/Governor appoint; PM/CM chair the respective committees.
points: The appointing authority acts only on the committee's recommendation.
Mixing the chair with the appointing authority is the usual trap.

POL-8.5.2-Q05.lead: The leader of the largest opposition group is deemed the LoP.
points: The Speaker and High Court judges have no role in this committee.
There is no Governor's nominee; the Governor only appoints.
POL-8.5.2-Q05.also: The same deeming rule applies to the Lok Sabha for the CIC committee.

POL-8.5.2-Q06.lead: Journalism and mass media is an eligibility field, not a bar.
points: MP/MLA membership, office of profit, and party/business/profession links all disqualify.
Eligible fields: law, S&T, social service, management, journalism, mass media, administration.

POL-8.5.2-Q07.lead: The Act keeps eligibility broad across many public-life fields.
points: No field is exclusive; civil servants are just one source.
No fixed degree or age qualification is laid down.

POL-8.5.2-Q08.lead: Post-2019 the Central Government prescribes the term, capped at 65.
points: The 2019 Amendment shifted the term from the statute to executive rules.
The age-65 cap continues.

POL-8.5.2-Q09.lead: The 2019 Rules prescribe three years, or till age 65.
points: Five years was the original statutory term, now removed.
Six years is the CEC/CAG-type term, not RTI.
POL-8.5.2-Q09.also: The same three-year term applies to State commissioners.

POL-8.5.2-Q10.lead: A follows from the 2019 Amendment; SIC is a state body.
points: SIC is appointed by the Governor and reports to the State Legislature.
The Centre controls its pay only because the RTI Act, as amended in 2019, says so.

POL-8.5.2-Q11.lead: No reappointment for the Chief; promotion allowed within a 5-year cap.
points: The bar on reappointment protects independence.
The aggregate cap stops extending tenure through promotion.

POL-8.5.2-Q12.lead: Note: the State Chief tracked an Election Commissioner, not the CEC.
points: Option 2 wrongly gives SCIC parity with the CEC.
All four parities were removed in 2019.

POL-8.5.2-Q13.lead: CIC Rs 2.5 lakh vs IC Rs 2.25 lakh; SCIC = SIC = Rs 2.25 lakh.
points: At state level the Rules give the same pay to Chief and members.
These figures are in Rules, which the Centre can change without Parliament.

POL-8.5.2-Q14.lead: This is the one 2005 safeguard that survived the 2019 Amendment.
points: Salary is prescribed by the Central Government, not the Commission or the Court.
Any change may only benefit a sitting commissioner.

POL-8.5.2-Q15.lead: The ceiling of ten ICs was not touched in 2019.
points: The 2019 changes apply alike to CIC and SIC.

POL-8.5.2-Q16.lead: Proved misbehaviour needs a Supreme Court enquiry first.
points: Insolvency, moral turpitude, outside employment, infirmity, prejudicial interest are direct grounds.
Misbehaviour and incapacity follow the separate SC route.

POL-8.5.2-Q17.lead: Even for state commissioners, the reference goes to the Supreme Court.
points: The High Court has no role here — a common trap.
The legislature does not vote on removal of Information Commissioners.
CIC has no supervisory power over SICs.

POL-8.5.2-Q18.lead: Insolvency is a direct ground; no enquiry needed.
points: Only misbehaviour and incapacity go to the Supreme Court.
The five direct grounds are decided by the President alone.

POL-8.5.2-Q19.lead: Interest as an ordinary member of an incorporated company is excluded.
points: Direct interest in a government contract or its profits is deemed misbehaviour.
The exception covers shareholding in common with other members.

POL-8.5.2-Q20.lead: Commission handles information-access grievances against public authorities only.
points: Other grounds: refusal, no reply in time, any other access matter.
Private consumer disputes go to consumer commissions.
POL-8.5.2-Q20.also: The Commission is also the second appellate authority under s.19.

POL-8.5.2-Q21.lead: No record may be withheld from the Commission on any ground.
points: Exemptions limit disclosure to the applicant, not to the Commission.
Suo motu power needs no complaint.

POL-8.5.2-Q22.lead: Civil-court powers make its inquiry quasi-judicial.
points: It can summon, take affidavits, order discovery and requisition records.
It cannot issue writs like a High Court.

POL-8.5.2-Q23.lead: The Commission can fine, not imprison.
points: Its penalty power is a monetary fine on the PIO.
Discovery/inspection of documents is also included.

POL-8.5.2-Q24.lead: Rs 250 per day, capped at Rs 25,000.
points: The fine is paid by the officer personally, not the department.
Disciplinary action may also be recommended.

POL-8.5.2-Q25.lead: 60 days x Rs 250 = Rs 15,000, below the Rs 25,000 cap.
points: Rs 25,000 is only the ceiling, reached at 100 days.
Rs 30,000 exceeds the statutory cap.

POL-8.5.2-Q26.lead: Compensation is a compliance power; recommendation is only advisory.
points: Compliance directions (s.19(8)) bind the authority.
Recommendations under s.25(5) are suggestions.

POL-8.5.2-Q27.lead: The Commission cannot dismiss officials; it can recommend disciplinary action.
points: It can also change record management, seek compliance reports, impose penalty.
It may reject an application as well.

POL-8.5.2-Q28.lead: Report goes via the government to the legislature.
points: The Commission submits it to the government, not directly to the House.
No report goes to the Supreme Court.

POL-8.5.2-Q29.lead: It secures information, not the underlying service.
points: First appeal lies to a senior officer in the same authority.
Second appeal to the Commission lies within 90 days.

POL-8.5.2-Q30.lead: DoPT under the Ministry of Personnel is the nodal agency.
points: I&B handles media, not RTI.
Law Ministry handles legislation drafting, not RTI implementation.
Samariya's term ended 13 Sept 2025.
The post stayed vacant for about three months.

POL-8.5.2-Q32.lead: Raj Kumar Goyal took oath on 15 December 2025.
points: Samariya's term ended in September 2025.
Y.K. Sinha preceded Samariya; Habibullah was the first CIC.
POL-8.5.2-Q32.also: Eight ICs sworn in with him took the CIC to full strength of 11.

POL-8.5.2-Q33.lead: Rs 10 fee; BPL applicants are exempt.
points: Copies cost Rs 2 per A4/A3 page.
Inspection is free for the first hour, then Rs 5 per 15 minutes.

POL-8.5.2-Q34.lead: AP charges no fee at village level.
points: Mandal level: Rs 5; division level and above: Rs 10.
Rs 2 per page is a copying charge, not an application fee.

POL-8.5.2-Q35.lead: First hour free; then Rs 5 per 15 minutes: 2 x Rs 5.
points: 30 extra minutes = two 15-minute blocks = Rs 10.
Rs 30 would wrongly charge for the free first hour.

POL-8.5.2-Q36.lead: Routine expenditure is ordinary disclosable information.
points: Section 8 exempts sovereignty, privilege, investigation, trade secrets, Cabinet papers etc.
Contempt-of-court material is also exempt.

POL-8.5.2-Q37.lead: Section 24 proviso carves out corruption and human rights.
points: Human-rights information is given only with the Commission's approval.
States can notify their own security bodies for exclusion.

POL-8.5.2-Q38.lead: The 2013 Bill lapsed; it never became law.
points: The Bill sought to override the CIC's June 2013 order on political parties.
It lapsed with the dissolution of the 15th Lok Sabha.

POL-8.5.2-Q39.lead: Public authority status brings a body within Section 2(h).
points: The government responded with the 2013 Amendment Bill to Section 2.
That Bill lapsed, so no amendment was made.

POL-8.5.2-Q41.lead: It meets once in three months.
points: Two RTI activists are nominated as members by the Collector.
Telangana's SIC was defunct from Feb 2023 till May 2025.

POL-8.5.2-Q43.lead: Vajja Srinivasa Rao, with four SICs, on 18 January 2026.
points: The AP Commission had been without a Chief before this.
Chandrasekhar Reddy heads Telangana's Commission.
P. Ramesh Kumar was AP SCIC from 2020.
POL-8.5.2-Q43.also: They hold office for three years or till 65, whichever earlier.

POL-8.5.2-Q44.lead: Executive control over term and pay is the basis of the criticism.
points: Government argued CIC is not comparable to a constitutional body like ECI.
Rules can be changed without going to Parliament.

POL-8.5.2-Q45.lead: Central PSUs fall within the CIC's jurisdiction, wherever located.
points: SIC covers only state government public authorities.
Courts and Collectors are not RTI appellate authorities.

POL-8.5.2-Q46.lead: SIC members are removed by the Governor, not the President.
points: Appointing and removing authority is the same at each level.

POL-8.5.2-Q47.lead: MPs and members of any state/UT legislature are barred.
points: The bar applies equally to Chief and members.
The Governor has no discretion to waive it.
Rules can only follow the parent Act's enabling power.
Eight ICs were sworn in on 15 Dec 2025 along with the CIC.
Ten is only the ceiling for ICs excluding the Chief.

POL-8.5.2-Q50.lead: Aggregate term as IC and CIC cannot exceed five years.
points: He also remains subject to the age-65 limit.
As Chief he cannot be reappointed afterwards.
Finland (1919) and Denmark (1955) followed later.
New Zealand (1962) was the first Commonwealth country, not the first overall.
POL-8.6.1-Q01.also: 'Ombud' is Swedish for one who speaks on another's behalf.

points: Denmark (1955) came after Finland (1919).
UK (1967) came after Norway (1962).
NZ and UK names are often swapped; NZ's word is 'Investigation'.
Lokpal is central; Lokayukta is state level.
France is the home of administrative courts (droit administratif).
Procurator was devised by socialist countries.

POL-8.6.1-Q05.lead: The Ombudsman reports; it cannot quash decisions.
points: Statement 1 is wrong: no power to reverse decisions or punish.
Rowat called it a bulwark against the 'tyranny of officialdom'.

POL-8.6.1-Q06.lead: The PC Act is of 1988; 1952 is the Commissions of Inquiry Act.
points: DSPE Act 1946 is the legal basis of the CBI.
CBI was set up in 1963, CVC in 1964 (Santhanam Committee).

POL-8.6.1-Q08.lead: Morarji Desai headed the First ARC initially (1966).
points: Veerappa Moily headed the Second ARC (2005).
Hanumanthaiah succeeded Desai as First ARC chairman later.

POL-8.6.1-Q09.lead: ARC excluded judiciary, following New Zealand, not Sweden.
points: Statement 3 is wrong: Swedish Ombudsman covers judges; ARC deliberately did not.

POL-8.6.1-Q10.lead: ARC wanted consultation with CJI, Speaker and RS Chairman.
points: PM-led Selection Committee is the 2013 Act design, not the ARC's.

POL-8.6.1-Q11.lead: The 1968 Bill lapsed when the 4th Lok Sabha was dissolved.
points: R correctly explains A.
Bills 1-4 and 6-8 all lapsed this way.
Nine attempts failed before it.

POL-8.6.1-Q14.lead: P.C. Ghose was the first Lokpal Chairperson, not a drafter.
points: Hazare, Hegde and Kejriwal were civil-society leaders of the 2011 movement.
The Jan Lokpal draft was largely not accepted by government.

POL-8.6.1-Q15.lead: Dec 2011 bill, 1 Jan 2014 assent, 16 Jan 2014 commencement, 2019 Chairperson.
points: Assent precedes commencement by 15 days.

POL-8.6.1-Q16.lead: Lokpal is created by the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013.
points: No Article of the Constitution provides for the Lokpal.

POL-8.6.1-Q17.lead: 50% quota is for SC/ST/OBC/minorities/women together, not women alone.

The quota is on members, not counting the Chairperson.

POL-8.6.1-Q19.lead: HC Chief Justice qualifies only as a judicial member.
points: Former CJI, former SC judge or eminent person can be Chairperson.

POL-8.6.1-Q20.lead: Act requires former SC judge or former HC Chief Justice.
points: An ordinary HC judge does not qualify.

POL-8.6.1-Q21.lead: RS Chairman is not on the 2013 Act's Selection Committee.
points: Members: PM (chair), Speaker, LoP in LS, CJI or nominee, eminent jurist.

POL-8.6.1-Q22.lead: Eminent jurist is nominated by the President, not the CJI.

POL-8.6.1-Q23.lead: The 50% rule for the Search Committee is the diversity extension.

POL-8.6.1-Q24.lead: The President appoints by warrant, and receives resignation.

PM only chairs the Selection Committee.

POL-8.6.1-Q25.lead: All three are disqualifications under the Act.
points: Members of local bodies, MPs and MLAs are barred.
